items.title: Fulfilling Our Nation’s Promise A Record 250 Identifications in Fiscal Year 2026
items.author: Courtesy
items.summary: DPAA has reached another identification milestone reaching 250 ID's in fiscal year 2026.
items.body:
WASHINGTON—Embodying the Warrior Ethos principle to “Never Leave a Fallen Comrade,” the Department of War, in Fiscal Year 2026, identified the remains of a milestone 250 Service members who had been unaccounted for from past conflicts.

This exceeds the previous record of 231 that the Defense POW/MIA Accounting Agency (DPAA) made in FY 2025.

The 250th to be identified is U.S. Army Capt. Albert P. Wilcox, a 39-year-old from California. He was a prisoner of war in the Philippines during World War II before being killed when the Japanese transport ship, Enoura Maru, was mistakenly sunk in 1945. Capt. Wilcox’ remains were recovered after the war but were unidentifiable, and he was buried as an Unknown. In 2022 DPAA began the *Enoura Maru *Project to disinter the Enoura Maru Unknowns from the National Memorial Cemetery of the Pacific and transferred them to the lab in Hawaii for identification. Capt Wilcox will be returned to his family who will decide on his final resting place. “The United States of America is resolved to never forget the warriors who answered the call to duty, made the supreme sacrifice, and never came home,” said Secretary of War Pete Hegseth. “Through DPAA’s determined efforts, all 250 of these heroes will finally be home.”

“This is a deeply personal priority for me,” said Hon. Anthony J. Tata, Under Secretary of War for personnel and readiness. “The Department of War will not rest in its efforts to bring home our unaccounted-for Service members and provide the fullest possible accounting of all mission personnel.”

DPAA is charged with searching for, recovering, and identifying Americans missing from past conflicts. These 250 accounted-for Service members include 198 from World War II, 51 from the Korean War, and one from the Vietnam War. Distributed among the branches of service, the identified Service members are: 136 U.S. Army, 76 U.S. Army Air Forces, 20 U.S. Navy, 15 U.S. Marine Corps, one U.S. Air Force, and 2 Federal Civilians.

Every unaccounted-for U.S. Service member or DoW civilian/contractor is entitled to one certainty: that he or she will not be forgotten. Operating in 54 countries around the world, the military and civilian professionals of DPAA are steadfastly committed to providing the fullest possible accounting of Americans missing from past conflicts to their families and the nation.

items.title: P-209 Dry Dock 5: Building toward dewatering
items.author: Jhewel Felipe
items.summary: Before the walls of the Navy’s newest dry dock can rise at Pearl Harbor Naval Shipyard, crews must build beneath the water. Steel piles driven deep into the harbor floor form the perimeter, while underwater concrete connects floor units to form the base. Together, these elements are creating the foundation for a facility designed to support submarine maintenance in the Pacific for generations.
items.body:
JOINT BASE PEARL HARBOR-HICKAM, Hawaii — Before the walls of the Navy’s newest dry dock can rise at Pearl Harbor Naval Shipyard, crews must build beneath the water. Steel piles driven deep into the harbor floor form the perimeter, while underwater concrete connects floor units to form the base. Together, these elements are creating the foundation for a facility designed to support submarine maintenance in the Pacific for generations.

This work marks the latest phase of a multiyear effort identified by the Department of the Navy as military construction project P-209 and will deliver the modern waterfront facility that will become Dry Dock 5. Dry docks are specialized structures where water is drained, allowing ships and submarines to undergo inspection, maintenance and repair while in the dry.

P-209 is being delivered through the Navy’s Shipyard Infrastructure Optimization Program (SIOP).

“SIOP is a comprehensive, long-term recapitalization effort that is delivering integrated investments in infrastructure and industrial plant equipment at the Navy’s four public shipyards, expanding shipyard capacity and optimizing shipyard configuration to meet the Navy’s nuclear-powered fleet maintenance requirements,” said Mark Edelson, program executive officer for Infrastructure and Expeditionary.

“As part of SIOP’s long-term, programmatic approach, our effort in building the new Dry Dock 5 includes lessons learned from previous megaprojects, and it is informing our approach to future megaprojects. All of this is part of our dedication to increase shipyard capacity and capability at our naval shipyards,” Edelson said.

Pearl Harbor Naval Shipyard & Intermediate Maintenance Facility (PHNSY & IMF) will operate the new facility once complete and certified. Meanwhile, Officer in Charge of Construction Pearl Harbor Naval Shipyard (OICC PHNSY) manages its construction.

OICC PHNSY is an echelon IV command under Naval Facilities Engineering Systems Command (NAVFAC) Pacific who oversees construction after contracts are awarded, monitors contractor compliance, quality and safety, and coordinates project activities among contractors, the shipyard and other government organizations.

When complete, Dry Dock 5 will transform years of complex construction into lasting maintenance capability for the Pacific Fleet.

“Dry Dock 5 will significantly upgrade our shipyard’s capabilities,” said Capt. Ryan McCrillis, PHNSY & IMF commander. “It replaces Dry Dock 3, which was built during World War II to accommodate vessels of that era. Because Dry Dock 3 is too shallow for newer, larger Virginia-class attack submarines, Dry Dock 5 will be the first dry dock built specifically for the latest nuclear submarines. It is designed to add another century of maintenance capability to PHNSY & IMF’s inventory, keeping the fleet combat-ready in the Pacific.”

Building from the harbor floor

Preparing the waterfront for construction required reshaping the site above and below the water. Crews dredged sediment from the harbor floor, created laydown and fabrication areas at Waipio Peninsula, near the shipyard for storing and organizing materials, and built a temporary trestle, a bridge-like work platform over the water. These early efforts established the network needed to move workers, equipment and massive dry dock components to the site.

The contractor developed an approach for creating a dry construction area within the harbor. Crews drive large steel pipe piles alongside interlocking steel panels called sheet piles to form a cofferdam. Once completed and reinforced, this temporary enclosure can be drained, allowing crews to build the permanent dry dock walls below the harbor’s waterline.

The dry dock floors began by taking shape on land, where crews built nine prefabricated concrete floor units at Waipio Peninsula. Each unit was transported by water and precisely lowered onto the harbor floor. Divers and concrete plant operators then worked together to place concrete underwater, connecting the floor units to the surrounding foundation.

Construction extends beyond the dock itself as P-209 includes utility systems, crane-rail foundations, pump stations, a water treatment system, an electrical substation and 10 supporting buildings. Together, these systems will provide power, drainage, crane access and operating space needed for Dry Dock 5.

Preparing for work in a dry environment

The project’s next major transition will be dewatering, the process of pumping water from the cofferdam, a temporary enclosure built in the harbor to keep the surrounding water out. Removing the water will create a dry workspace for the next stage of construction.

Once the water is removed, the foundation constructed beneath the harbor will come into view. Crews can then begin building the permanent walls, moving P-209 into its next major stage.

“The ongoing preparations for dewatering are the most important and dangerous part of the project,” said Capt. Chris Coggins, OICC PHNSY commanding officer. “Without completing this phase, workers will not be able to safely enter or build at a depth of 60 feet below the adjacent waterline.”

Reinforcing the enclosure

Once the water inside the cofferdam is removed, the temporary enclosure must withstand pressure from the surrounding harbor.

“First, the perimeter cofferdam pile driving needs to be completed and inspected,” said Coggins. “This provides the bathtub and door to safely keep the water out.”

Crews build the perimeter downward in stages. They drive one steel pile section into the harbor floor, weld another section on top and continue driving until the pile reaches its required depth. Inside the cofferdam, braces and struts connect the parallel walls, helping them resist pressure from the surrounding water.

Beside the cofferdam, crews are building the pump well, which will contain the equipment used to drain Dry Dock 5 during future vessel maintenance. Below the surface, crews are also placing concrete through tremie pipes, which allow concrete to be delivered underwater. The concrete connects the prefabricated floor units to the perimeter while the construction area remains flooded.

One Navy effort

Delivering Dry Dock 5 depends on more than the work taking place at the waterfront. The project brings together organizations responsible for funding, construction oversight, shipyard operations, labor and material support.

“Just as we rely on the broader Navy enterprise for guidance and parts to maintain submarines, we rely on NAVFAC, SIOP and industry partners to deliver Dry Dock 5,” McCrillis said. “This unified effort will ensure we have the facility needed to keep the Pacific Fleet ‘Fit to Fight.’”

The construction workforce is expected to grow from approximately 350 workers per day to more than 1,000 as the project enters its next phase. That growth will increase demand for skilled labor, concrete and other locally supplied materials, connecting the project’s construction needs with Hawaii’s workforce and industrial base.

“This type of megaproject requires continued collaboration and coordination among all team members,” Coggins said. “Teamwork with local unions and batch plant operators to prioritize supplies will be key to the project’s success.”

While the construction workforce builds the facility, PHNSY & IMF personnel are preparing to operate it. Shipyard employees participate in design, testing and planning for future operations, while workforce programs help prepare future employees for careers supporting the Navy’s maintenance mission.

“Our shipyard personnel are not just waiting for Dry Dock 5 to be built; they are actively involved in the design, testing and planning for future operations, ensuring we can begin maintaining submarines when it is completed,” McCrillis said. “We have many pathways to become part of our shipyard ‘ohana. The most popular is our Apprenticeship Program, which opens each year to approximately 150 new employees who learn a trade while earning a degree.”

Dry Dock 5 also reflects NAVFAC Pacific’s broader responsibility for delivering and sustaining defense infrastructure throughout the region.

“The mission of NAVFAC Pacific is to deliver infrastructure that enables the Fleet and Joint Force to deter, fight, and win,” said Rear Adm. Omarr Tobias, NAVFAC Pacific commander. “We do that by employing construction, engineering, and contracting expertise across the Pacific theater.”

“We are the engineering support to the Fleet. From constructing piers and runways to ensuring clean water and power at bases, we make sure our warfighters have the infrastructure they need to succeed—wherever they’re called to serve.”

That mission depends on skilled engineers, construction managers, program and project managers, architects, engineering technicians and contract specialists working across the Pacific area of operations.

“The Pacific requires disciplined speed, theater-wide portfolio thinking, and a government and industry co-created delivery ecosystem, from the expeditionary edge to the Foundry. The job ahead is massive, but the stakes are high.” Tobias said. “Peace, deterrence, and stability across the Pacific depend directly on the speed, durability, and resilience of the infrastructure we put in place today, from austere airfields to our largest dry docks. Our work must deliver the right capability – ready when the Joint Force needs it.”

items.title: Two Dover Airmen Sentenced in Multimillion-Dollar Cyber Fraud Scheme
items.author: Todd South
items.summary: A federal judge recently sentenced one Airman and a former Airman to a combined 15 years in prison and ordered them to pay $1.36 million in restitution for a two-year cyber fraud scheme they perpetrated while serving on Active-Duty at Dover Air Force Base, Del. The post Two Dover Airmen Sentenced in Multimillion-Dollar Cyber Fraud Scheme appeared first on Air & Space Forces Magazine .
items.body:
A federal judge recently sentenced one Airman and a former Airman to a combined 15 years in prison and ordered them to pay $1.36 million in restitution for a two-year cyber fraud scheme they perpetrated while serving on Active-Duty at Dover Air Force Base, Del.

On Sept. 25, Chijioke Timothy Odimegwu, 25, and Harafat Mogaji, 26, were sentenced to nine years, three months, and six years, six months in federal prison, respectively, for their role in a cyber fraud scheme that targeted at least 15 businesses, towns, and nonprofits while also conducting romance fraud schemes to get victims to act as “money mules” for their more than $2.4 million in stolen funds.

Neither man was involved in cyber career fields in the Air Force.

Odimegwu and Mogaji previously pleaded guilty to charges of conspiracy to commit wire fraud, conspiracy to commit access device fraud, and aggravated identity theft.

The Air Force Office of Special Investigations’ Detachment 306 at Dover assisted the FBI in the investigation. The detachment, a local field unit, helped identify victims, investigated threats made by the defendants, and conducted federal arrests of the two Airmen, according to an AFOSI release.

“This case demonstrates why strong partnerships across law enforcement are critical to protecting the Department of the Air Force and the American people,” said Special Agent Kevin Golden, commander of the detachment.

Mogaji was discharged from the USAF earlier this year; as of his recent sentencing, Odimegwu was still awaiting discharge.

Airman First Class Odimegwu joined the Air Force in February 2023, became a Traffic Management Apprentice, and last served as a household goods specialist, according to an Air Force spokesperson. His awards include the Air Force Training Ribbon, Air Force Outstanding Unit Award, and the Air Force Good Conduct Medal.

Mogaji served from 2022 to July 4, 2026. His terminal rank was Airman First Class; he was a services apprentice and last served as a fitness and sports journeyman. His awards include the Air Force Training Ribbon, the Global War on Terrorism Service Medal, the Air Force Outstanding Unit Award, the Air Force Good Conduct Medal, and the Air Force Longevity Service Award.

According to court documents, the pair spoofed the victims’ email addresses with similar addresses, gained username and password access to the victims’ accounts, and then monitored them for large financial transactions.

“Cyber-enabled crime does not stop at installation boundaries or geographic borders,” Golden said. “Working alongside our federal partners allows us to identify threats, protect our personnel and resources, and hold those responsible accountable.”

In one instance, the pair targeted a victim in Iowa City, Iowa, and were able to gain access to a $1.68 million wire transfer the nonprofit was using for a construction project and divert it to a Chicago bank account.

In another example, the pair phished an official from the City of Athens, Ohio, intercepted a $720,000 wire transfer, and used a romance scam victim as the money mule to take the initial transfer before moving it to their own accounts.

“The city has received $205,000 to date in recovered stolen funds and a $200,000 insurance payout,” Mayor Steve Patterson said at a Sept. 28 city council meeting.In late 2025, the city adopted a state-recommended cybersecurity policy that outlines specific procedures for electronic payments.

“Criminals from all backgrounds attack our digital systems. They strike targets from corporate networks to personal smartphones,” Eugene Kowel, Special Agent in Charge of the FBI Omaha Field Office, said in a Department of Justice release. “No one and no device is immune from the threat. This case demonstrates that we will hold accountable cybercriminals who target our communities. It also serves as a reminder that every organization and every individual should take steps to protect their devices and systems and learn how to recognize and avoid scams.”

items.title: 26th MEU Forms Complete MAGTF Ahead of Kearsarge ARG Deployment
items.author: 1LT Luke Lindsey
items.summary: MARINE CORPS BASE CAMP LEJEUNE, N.C. — The 26th Marine Expeditionary Unit completed its composite Sept. 28, bringing together its command, ground, aviation and logistics combat elements as a Marine Air-Ground Task Force ahead of its upcoming deployment with the Kearsarge Amphibious Ready Group.
items.body:
MARINE CORPS BASE CAMP LEJEUNE, N.C. — The 26th Marine Expeditionary Unit completed its composite Sept. 28, bringing together its command, ground, aviation and logistics combat elements as a Marine Air-Ground Task Force ahead of its upcoming deployment with the Kearsarge Amphibious Ready Group.

The composite brings Battalion Landing Team 1st Battalion, 8th Marines, serving as the ground combat element; Marine Medium Tiltrotor Squadron 261 (reinforced), serving as the aviation combat element; and Combat Logistics Battalion 22, serving as the logistics combat element, under the 26th MEU Command Element. Together, the four elements provide the command and control, ground combat, aviation and logistics capabilities that enable the 26th MEU to operate as an integrated MAGTF.

“The 26th MEU, call sign Proteus, grew larger as a family after compositing the command element, ground, aviation and logistics Marines and Sailors as one integrated MAGTF. We look forward to the pre-deployment program, where we will integrate with our naval counterparts at PHIBRON 4 to build warfighting readiness and capabilities to provide combatant commanders an all-domain, adaptable and lethal sea-based force. Team Proteus will come to fight and win and live up to our mantra, ‘A Certain Force in an Uncertain World,’” said Col. Michael Stansberry, commanding officer of the 26th MEU.

Prior to composite, the MEU’s major subordinate elements conducted individual and unit-level training to build proficiency within their respective mission sets. Now composited, the 26th MEU enters the next phase of its pre-deployment training program, focused on integrating and evaluating the MAGTF as a cohesive force. Marines and Sailors across the MAGTF will train together through progressively complex events designed to build interoperability and prepare the MEU for deployment.

Lt. Gen. Robert C. Fulford, commanding general of II Marine Expeditionary Force, emphasized the MEF’s responsibility to ensure the 26th MEU is properly equipped, trained and prepared for its upcoming deployment. “Our responsibility at the MEF is to ensure the MEU has the right personnel, equipment, capabilities and training to accomplish its mission,” Fulford said. “The pre-deployment training program is a time-tested process. We must trust that process while remaining flexible enough to address emerging opportunities and challenges.”

This iteration of the 26th MEU will also integrate capabilities not previously deployed with the unit. The upcoming deployment will mark the first time the 26th MEU deploys with the Amphibious Combat Vehicle, CH-53K King Stallion and F-35B Lightning II. The MEU will also employ Organic Precision Fires-Light, providing infantry formations with a portable loitering munition capability that combines reconnaissance, surveillance and target acquisition with precision strike.

With its major subordinate elements now composited, the 26th MEU will continue through its pre-deployment training program and future deployment, increasing naval integration while embarked aboard the USS Kearsarge (LHD 3), USS Arlington (LPD 24) and USS Tortuga (LSD 46). Throughout the workup, Expeditionary Operations Training Group, Expeditionary Warfare Training Group Atlantic and Amphibious Squadron 4 will support the training and evaluation of the MEU through progressively complex events designed to assess its ability to plan, integrate and execute assigned mission essential tasks. These events will provide opportunities to identify and refine processes as the 26th MEU and PHIBRON 4 build proficiency as an integrated ARG/MEU team.

The 26th MEU’s upcoming deployment contributes to the Marine Corps’ goal of restoring a 3.0 ARG/MEU presence, which calls for one MEU forward from the East Coast, one from the West Coast and the 31st MEU deploying from Okinawa. During the 2026 Modern Day Marine Final Keynote Address in Washington, Gen. Eric M. Smith, commandant of the Marine Corps, identified returning to a 3.0 ARG/MEU presence as his “North Star.” Smith also described the ARG/MEU as a “force of choice for Combatant Commanders,” providing a forward-deployed and responsive capability across the competition continuum.

The 26th Marine Expeditionary Unit, coupled with the USS Kearsarge Amphibious Ready Group, provides geographic combatant commanders with a flexible, sea-based naval expeditionary force capable of conducting amphibious operations, crisis response, maritime interdiction and contingency response operations. The integrated ARG/MEU team combines maritime mobility with aviation, ground combat, logistics and command-and-control capabilities across a range of military operations, in any clime and place.

items.title: OA-1K Goes Off Runway at Oklahoma Airport; Crew Safe
items.author: Greg Hadley
items.summary: An OA-1K Skyraider II belonging to Air Force Special Operations Command went off the runway while landing at a small Oklahoma City airport Oct. 5 and is waiting to be moved, according to officials and flight tracking data. The post OA-1K Goes Off Runway at Oklahoma Airport; Crew Safe appeared first on Air & Space Forces Magazine .
items.body:
An OA-1K Skyraider II belonging to Air Force Special Operations Command went off the runway while landing at a small Oklahoma City airport Oct. 5 and is waiting to be moved, according to officials and flight tracking data.

Local media outlets first reported on the incident, which occurred at Sundance Airport about 20 miles from Will Rogers Air National Guard Base where the plane took off.

The two crew members on board are safe, a spokesperson for the 492nd Special Operations Wing confirmed to Air & Space Forces Magazine.

The incident occurred during a training sortie just a few days after the 492nd announced on social media that the OA-1K’s formal training unit had started training its first class of new pilots. The wing spokesperson declined to say whether one of the new student pilots was on board during the incident.

The OA-1K is a “combat scout” adapted from a cropduster that Air Force special operators plan to use for light attack and intelligence, surveillance, and reconnaissance missions in less contested airspace, particularly for counterinsurgency operations. The first airframe arrived at Will Rogers in June 2025, and test and instructor pilots have spent the past year preparing the “schoolhouse” to train special ops aviators.

According to flight tracking data, the OA-1K involved in the incident took off from Will Rogers in the mid-afternoon of Oct. 5 and flew patterns for several hours before coming in to land at Sundance Airport. About midway down the runway, the aircraft veered to its left and came to rest in the grass.

“The 492nd Special Operations Wing is tracking an incident involving one of its OA-1K Skyraider II aircraft at Sundance Airport, Oklahoma City,” the wing spokesperson said. “Both crew members are safe and the cause of the incident is under investigation. Further details will follow as the investigation develops.”

Citing the Oklahoma City Fire Department, local TV station News 9 reported that the aircraft “nose-dived” as it was landing and its propeller was damaged. Another TV station, KOCO News 5, released video of the aircraft after the incident, appearing to show its propeller blades bent and skid marks in the grass behind it.

The 492nd spokesperson said that, as of the morning of Oct. 6, the aircraft remains at Sundance Airport.

“Our team is currently working courses of action to remove the aircraft off the airfield. Safety-trained personnel are on scene documenting and collecting all evidence while developing a plan to remove the aircraft as soon as safety-investigative procedures allow,” the spokesperson said.

While the OA-1K formal training unit just started its first class of new pilots, this is the second safety incident involving the Skyraider II since it arrived in Oklahoma. In October 2025, an experienced special ops aviator making the transition to the OA-1K inadvertently shut off the plane’s fuel in the middle of a training sortie, leading to the aircraft flying extremely low over a local road before crashing in a field.

items.title: Air Force’s Hypersonic Attack Cruise Missile Has First Flight Test
items.author: Todd South
items.summary: The U.S. Air Force has conducted the first flight test release of its developing hypersonic cruise missile, with that test taking place in Australia. The post Air Force’s Hypersonic Attack Cruise Missile Has First Flight Test appeared first on Air & Space Forces Magazine .
items.body:
The U.S. Air Force has conducted the first flight test release of its developing hypersonic cruise missile, with that test taking place in Australia.

An Air Force spokesperson confirmed to Air & Space Forces Magazine on Oct. 6 that the Hypersonic Attack Cruise Missile flight test had occurred. The spokesperson did not specify a date.

The HACM flight test happened over a “designated Australian test range, gathering crucial data to advance the program’s objectives,” according to the spokesperson. The Woomera Test Range in the desert of southern Australia is commonly used to test missiles, aircraft, and projectiles.

The War Zone first reported on the test on Oct. 5.

“This effort is part of the Southern Cross Integrated Flight Research Experiment, a collaborative agreement built on more than 15 years of partnership between our two nations,” the spokesperson wrote in an email.

The spokesperson declined to provide further details regarding the method of test, platform used to conduct the test, flight times, durations, or speed.

RTX, the prime contractor on the missile, deferred any comments to the Air Force. Northrop Grumman, the missile’s engine-maker, did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

HACM came out of a Defense Advanced Research Projects Agency program to develop a concept for a hypersonic air-breathing weapon and traces its origins to the Boeing X-51 Wave Rider project.

In April 2020, the Air Force issued an industry call for proposals on the potential weapon. It formally established the HACM program in 2022, picking RTX for the munition and Northrop for the scramjet engine.

HACM is one of two hypersonic weapons the Air Force is pursuing, along with the larger AGM-183 Air-Launched Rapid Response Weapon, or ARRW.

The munition uses a conventional rocket booster to reach high speeds, then ditches it and engages the scramjet engine to reach and maintain speeds above Mach 5, or 3,300 miles per hour, at high altitudes.

HACM recently saw a yearlong delay because of design problems, and the Air Force cut its flight count for rapid-prototyping tests from seven to five. A 2024 GAO report said the program had a “zero margin” in its development timeline at the time, and it has since been declared behind schedule and over its original budget.

USAF is seeking about $1.2 billion to mature and field the missile in its fiscal 2027 budget proposal. It has also asked for a dedicated production line for the missile and requested $404 million for the first operational lot.

The Air Force plans to begin fielding HACM in fiscal 2027 and expects to move it to full-rate production by fiscal 2029.

items.title: Arctic Security Research Takes Cadets Beyond The Classroom
items.author: SSgt Michael Ward
items.summary: U.S. Air Force Academy cadets explored Arctic security through the Homeland Defense Institute (HDI), researching Russian and Chinese activity in the region and engaging with military organizations, researchers and regional stakeholders across Alaska.
items.body:
Cadet 1st Class Katherine Longuil, left, and Cadet 1st Class Gavin Dustin, right, walk beneath a B-52 Stratofortress at the U.S. Air Force Academy, Colo., Sept. 16, 2026. As part of their Homeland Defense Institute experience, the cadets explored strategic bombing and its role in the broader history of homeland defense.

By SSgt Michael Ward U.S. Air Force Academy Strategic Communications

U.S. AIR FORCE ACADEMY, Colo. –U.S. Air Force Academy cadets explored Arctic security through the Homeland Defense Institute (HDI), researching Russian and Chinese activity in the region and engaging with military organizations, researchers and regional stakeholders across Alaska.

The Homeland Defense Institute is a collaboration between the Academy, the North American Aerospace Defense Command and U.S. Northern Command focused on advancing homeland defense through strategic education, research and partnerships.

For this experience, HDI partnered with the Ted Stevens Center for Arctic Security Studies, which oversees the cadets’ research and connects them with Arctic security experts and organizations.

Connecting cadets with homeland defense missions

HDI connects cadets with homeland defense organizations and missions through partnerships across the Arctic and High North.

Jesse L. Johnson Jr., deputy director of HDI, said these experiences help cadets develop an understanding of homeland defense that extends beyond concepts taught in the classroom.

“Experiential research is essential to HDI’s mission because it transforms homeland defense from an abstract concept into lived understanding,” said Johnson. “These experiences expose cadets to real operational environments, real stakeholders and real challenges, something no classroom can fully replicate.”

Cadet 1st Class Gavin Dustin’s interest in Russian and Eastern European history began after he was assigned Russian to fulfill his foreign language requirement during his freshman year. Now a Foreign Area Studies major with a minor in Russian, Dustin used the research opportunity to apply his academic interests to Arctic security research.

In Alaska, Dustin helped develop a website focused on current Russian ambitions and capabilities in the Arctic.

Additionally, he visited military installations and communities throughout the state, including Joint Base Elmendorf-Richardson, Nome and Utqiagvik.

Studying strategic competition in the Arctic

While Dustin focused on Russian activity in the Arctic, Cadet 1st Class Katherine Longuil studied China’s activity in the region.

“I engaged with a plethora of sources and people to learn more about the history of what China has done in the Arctic, what they are currently doing, how China engages with Russia and what that could mean,” said Longuil.

Johnson said the Arctic is one of HDI’s three core focus areas because of its growing importance to strategic competition.

“The Arctic is one of HDI’s three core focus areas because it is rapidly becoming a decisive arena for strategic competition,” said Johnson. “It is not just a remote region. It is a frontline.”

Johnson said the region’s geography, resources and increasing military and commercial activity have made it an important area of study for homeland defense. Changes in Arctic accessibility are also increasing opportunities for competitors to operate near North America, he said.

Studying those issues in Alaska gave cadets an opportunity to connect geopolitical concepts with the Arctic’s physical and cultural environment.

Learning beyond the classroom

Traveling through Alaska allowed Dustin to see cultural and geographic similarities between Alaska and the Russian region he had studied academically.

“I learned how many ways Siberia and Alaska are really the same part of the world,” said Dustin. “There was something about seeing the Orthodox crosses in rural Alaska, hearing Russian spoken on the street, being in the forest of Denali and realizing that it’s the same forest that’s over in Russia.”

Dustin also visited the former Nike Missile Site on Joint Base Elmendorf-Richardson, where a conversation with a soldier who had been stationed there during the Cold War gave him insight into the threat posed by Soviet bombers and how homeland defense challenges have evolved over time.

“It was really striking to speak to a soldier who was stationed there during the Cold War and realize how real of a threat Soviet bombers were in the early Cold War,” said Dustin.

Longuil gained a different perspective through interactions with Arctic security researchers. When she encountered difficulty identifying connections between China and the Arctic, another researcher studying the region helped her develop a broader strategic context.

“He gave me phenomenal mentorship that helped me make some much larger connections and see the bigger picture from a strategic aspect,” said Longuil.

Johnson said those interactions help cadets develop skills that extend beyond research itself.

“Classroom instruction can teach concepts, but experiences like this teach perspective,” said Johnson. “Cadets gain operational realism, interagency and binational exposure, applied problem-solving and strategic awareness.”

Preparing future homeland defenders

The experience also shaped how cadets view the responsibilities they will assume after commissioning.

Longuil said studying homeland defense in an operational environment helped her recognize the importance of working across organizations and communicating with partners as an officer.

“Being able to research through HDI has given me lots of real-world experience, getting to sit in on upper echelon briefings and learning how to make cross branch connections,” said Longuil. “I didn’t realize how much officership was joint force work and strategic communications with others, which has prepared me even more to commission.”

Dustin said his experience in Alaska also changed how he views the Arctic’s role in international relations.

“My experience in Alaska has made me much more cognizant of the growing importance of the Arctic region,” said Dustin. “I think it is a part of the world that is often overlooked in discussions of international relations.” Johnson said experiences like these give cadets early exposure to the complexity of homeland defense and help prepare them to operate across the defense enterprise.

“By engaging directly with NORAD and USNORTHCOM mission partners, cadets gain the mindset and skills required to operate in a dynamic security environment,” said Johnson. “They leave with a deeper understanding of the homeland they will soon be responsible for defending.”

items.title: Air University researchers, educators earn AETC STEM honors
items.author: Billy Blankenship
items.summary: Air University researchers, educators and STEM contributors earned six AETC-level honors in the 2026 Science, Technology, Engineering and Mathematics Awards. The winners represent work spanning advanced space research, human digital twin technology, engineering, education and STEM outreach, highlighting how AU expertise is helping solve operational problems while developing the next generation of warfighters. All six recipients advance to compete at the Department of the Air Force level.
items.body: MAXWELL AIR FORCE BASE, Ala. -- A technical idea matters when the force can put it to work. Six Air University researchers, educators and STEM contributors earned Air Education and Training Command-level honors in the 2026 Science, Technology, Engineering and Mathematics Awards. Their work reaches across research, engineering, education and outreach. Five of the winners are from the Air Force Institute of Technology at Wright-Patterson Air Force Base, Ohio. The sixth is from Squadron Officer School at Maxwell Air Force Base. The work isn't the same, and that's part of the value. "What stands out to me is the range of work being recognized," said Col. James Bowers, AFIT Acting Director and Chancellor. "These awards represent researchers, engineers and educators who are committed to solving the Joint Force's toughest technical challenges while forging warrior scholars through our academic programs. That's what AFIT provides the Department of War. We cultivate technical expertise, then deliver it to help Airmen address current operational needs and strengthen the Joint Force." Capt. Guillermo A. Salcedo, AFIT/ENG, was named AETC's Outstanding Scientist/Engineer in the mid-career military category. Sean A. Gunther, AFIT/ENS, earned the Engineering Technician award, while AFIT's Human Digital Twin Ontology Team received the Outstanding Scientist/Engineer Team Award. Daniel F. Koranek, AFIT/ENG, earned the Outstanding Science and Engineering Educator Award, and Lt. Col. Robert A. Bettinger, AFIT/ENY, received the Air Force Research and Development Award. The five AFIT selections cover different disciplines, but they point toward the same question: How can technical knowledge help solve a problem for the warfighter? New technology by itself doesn't answer that question. Someone has to understand it, test it, figure out where it falls short and determine whether it actually helps the force do something better. The Human Digital Twin Ontology Team's work brings that idea into focus. Today's systems don't always have a common way to understand the physical and cognitive condition of the person operating them. The AFIT team is developing a shared framework for representing that information digitally, laying groundwork for human digital twins that could eventually help track operator performance, fatigue and environmental stress across different systems and models. The team is developing two ontologies, each representing human information in a different operational context, and combining what they have in common into a broader framework. The work builds on baseline standards from the Chief Digital and Artificial Intelligence Office Council and the Intelligence Community Chief Data Officer Council. "Systems often operate with zero visibility into the operator's real-time physical or cognitive limits," said Capt. Cameron McGrath, AFIT/ENV. "We're establishing a shared understanding of the human and their digital counterpart that can span different tools, AI agents and engineering models." The goal is eventually to allow systems to better account for the person operating them, giving warfighters and commanders better information about performance, fatigue, environmental stress and readiness. Bettinger's work shows another way Air University research can connect with a problem the force is trying to solve. His research focuses in part on operating beyond traditional near-Earth orbits. Bettinger co-authored a 350-page book on space situational awareness, navigation and communications architectures for multi-body environments, including cislunar space and Mars. The book will support two AFIT graduate courses in cislunar trajectory and mission design. Those courses have evolved in response to Air Force Research Laboratory requirements. Bettinger and his students are now using higher-fidelity dynamics models to develop trajectory solutions for AFRL while preparing graduates to move into assignments involving cislunar mission planning and trajectory development. The research extends beyond trajectory design. Bettinger received $500,000 in defense research grants supporting work in multi-body dynamics, cislunar trajectories, transforming satellite structures, rapid point-to-point cargo delivery and space-object conjunction analysis. The work supports AFRL efforts ranging from on-orbit trajectory and remote-sensing capabilities to reducing unnecessary collision-avoidance maneuvers that consume spacecraft propellant. Bettinger also received two U.S. patents related to satellite payloads and structures. One uses cubic origami structures to compactly fold deployable arrays or mirror surfaces inside satellites. The other addresses satellite structures capable of articulation and transformation. His team is now extending that work toward large transforming truss structures for future on-orbit platforms. The connection between the research and the classroom is deliberate. Bettinger has graduated eight master's students and currently works with five master's and two doctoral students. The same problems being studied for AFRL are helping prepare space professionals who may eventually work those problems in operational and technical assignments. Getting a good idea out of research and into the hands of the force isn't just about moving faster. Someone still has to determine whether a new technology actually solves the problem it was built to address. Sometimes that means testing an idea and finding out the first answer wasn't the right one. That's useful, too. Air University's STEM work doesn't stop with advanced technical research. At Maxwell, Maj. Joseph S. Kohan of Squadron Officer School was named AETC's Individual Outreach Volunteer for the STEM Outreach Award. As aerospace education officer for Civil Air Patrol Squadron AL-032 at Maxwell, Kohan leads hands-on STEM programs for 60 cadets from Montgomery and communities across central Alabama. His work ranges from rocketry and aviation weather to flight planning and high-altitude balloon experiments. For the Civil Air Patrol Joe Kittinger High-Altitude Balloon Challenge, Kohan spent 15 hours developing training and mentoring 24 cadets as they used the scientific method to design payloads capable of surviving conditions in the stratosphere. The Alabama CAP Wing commander also selected him to set up and develop a training program for a $9,000 aviation simulator supporting the wing's 25 pilots and 13 aircraft, while providing aviation ground training to Maxwell cadets. For Kohan, the work is personal. His own path to the Air Force began in high school through Air Force Junior ROTC, where his aerospace science instructors helped set him on a path to the U.S. Air Force Academy and, eventually, pilot training. "Without them, I do not think I would be where I am today," Kohan said. "I am trying to return that favor to our current generation of cadets." Kohan said his work with Civil Air Patrol cadets isn't about producing immediate results. It's about introducing STEM early enough to help shape where a young person may eventually go. "It's about steady, intentional course adjustments," Kohan said. "Over time, those small nudges compound into exponential growth." Taken together, the six winners give a snapshot of the range of work happening across Air University. Some of it starts with a technical problem. Some starts in a classroom. Some begins years before an Airman ever has to make a decision with the knowledge being developed today. The real test is whether any of it gets used. Did the work help someone see a problem differently? Did it inform a decision? Did it improve readiness or give a warfighter another way to accomplish the mission? Those questions matter more than the number of papers written, courses completed or awards received. Getting research in front of operators, planners and decision-makers is one side of it. Bringing their problems back to the people who teach, study and research them is the other. That back-and-forth gives Air University researchers a clearer picture of what the force needs and gives the force another place to turn when the answer isn't obvious. And the answer won't always be obvious. Threats change. Technology changes. A problem can change before the force finishes solving it. That puts a premium on people who can recognize the change, ask a better question and test a different answer. The six AETC STEM winners are one snapshot of those people at work. Their accomplishments span research, engineering, education and outreach. What ties them together isn't the award. It's what their expertise can do next. For Air University, that's where the recognition connects to the larger mission: forging expert joint warfighters and helping solve operational problems for the Joint Force. All six Air University recipients now advance to compete at the Department of the Air Force level.

items.title: The G.O.A.T. approach to wildfire mitigation.
items.author: Oscar Garcia
items.summary: MCAS Miramar’s Marine Corps-funded Operation Goat Rope pilot is using 471 goats to reduce wildfire fuels in steep, hard-to-access terrain. Supported by NAVFAC EXWC and evaluated with the Texas A&M Natural Resources Institute, the project will compare prescribed grazing with chemical and mechanical vegetation-management methods to determine whether it can provide a safe, effective, and scalable tool for installation wildfire resilience.
items.body:
At first glance, the 471 goats moving across the dry, rugged hills of Marine Corps Air Station (MCAS) Miramar may look like an unusual answer to Southern California’s wildfire threat, but the program is a calculated, Marine Corps-funded effort led by MCAS Miramar that NAVFAC EXWC is helping evaluate.

Dubbed Operation Goat Rope by MCAS Miramar, NAVFAC EXWC awarded the pilot designed to determine whether prescribed grazing can give military installations a safer, adaptable, and potentially cost-effective way to reduce hazardous vegetation before it becomes fuel for a wildfire.

At MCAS Miramar, the herd is grazing in East Miramar, an area where steep terrain and dense vegetation can make mechanical brush removal difficult and hazardous for crews. By consuming dry brush, invasive grasses, and other vegetation, the goats are helping reduce fuels in locations that can be challenging to manage with heavy equipment.

The effort supports MCAS Miramar’s broader fire-prevention strategy and could eventually contribute to fuel breaks along the installation’s perimeter. Those fuel breaks may help protect military infrastructure while reducing wildfire risk for neighboring communities, including Scripps Ranch and Tierrasanta.

“Texas A&M Natural Resources Institute [is] providing us academic research capability to validate whether this works,” said Jesse Ross of NAVFAC EXWC.

The goats are the visible part of the project. The research behind them is what could shape future decisions.

Along with the Marines, NAVFAC EXWC is partnering with the Texas A&M Natural Resources Institute to collect and analyze data from the Miramar pilot. The Marine Corps funded the effort, while MCAS Miramar is hosting and leading the project on the ground. The purpose is to compare prescribed grazing with other vegetation-management approaches, including chemical treatment and mechanical removal, and determine whether grazing can meet installation fuel-reduction needs while limiting impacts on sensitive habitat and reducing reliance on heavy machinery.

“The primary goals are to collect the data and compare grazing as an effective tool versus other options like chemical treatment and mechanical removal,” said Jesse Ross of NAVFAC EXWC. “Does grazing provide us a solution?”

That question is at the center of the pilot’s strategic value. Installations in wildfire-prone regions must balance several requirements at once: protecting people and mission infrastructure, maintaining access to difficult terrain, managing environmental considerations, and using available resources. Prescribed grazing may offer an additional option for installation leaders, but NAVFAC EXWC’s role is to help determine where, when, and under what conditions it works.

The Miramar pilot is being closely monitored because it combines an established land-management practice with a formal research framework. Rather than treating grazing as a one-time demonstration, the project is intended to produce defensible findings that installations can use when considering future wildfire-mitigation investments.

Ross said the project reflects NAVFAC EXWC’s role in enabling customers to test promising approaches and use the results to inform future decisions. “EXWC enabled this pilot to test if a new approach can work, and then our customers can take the findings and decide whether to scale up.”

If the data supports broader use, the Miramar project could provide a model for other installations confronting similar wildfire risks. That is the intended path for NAVFAC EXWC innovation efforts: support installation-led initiatives, test promising capabilities under real conditions, validate the results, and provide customers with information they can use to make informed decisions.

At Miramar, the goats are reducing hazardous fuels one mouthful at a time. Behind them, Marines, scientists, engineers, firefighters, and installation partners are building the evidence needed to help protect missions, communities, and landscapes across the force.

items.title: Twentynine Palms immunization training prepares Sailors to support medical readiness
items.author: Christopher Jones
items.summary: Navy Medicine Readiness and Training Command Twentynine Palms trained 34 Sailors during its first Basic Vaccinator Course at Naval Hospital Twentynine Palms, Sept. 24, 2026. The training combined classroom instruction, hands-on skills stations and competency testing to prepare Sailors to safely administer vaccines, screen patients, respond to adverse reactions and properly document care. Developed by Hospital Corpsman 1st Class Peter Amponsah, the course brought together personnel from across th
items.body:
TWENTYNINE PALMS, Calif. — Thirty-four Sailors from across Navy Medicine Readiness and Training Command (NMRTC) Twentynine Palms and supporting operational units completed the command’s first Basic Vaccinator Course on Sept. 24, expanding the number of personnel qualified to administer vaccines and strengthening the command’s ability to support force health protection and medical readiness.

The training combined classroom instruction, hands-on practice and competency testing to prepare participants to safely administer vaccines, screen patients, respond to adverse reactions and properly document immunizations.

Hospital Corpsman 1st Class Peter Amponsah, a preventive medicine technician and leading petty officer for the command’s preventive medicine department, developed the training after arriving at NMRTC Twentynine Palms and identifying an opportunity to expand vaccination capabilities across the command.

For Amponsah, the idea had its roots in training he received eight years earlier.

“The idea grew from my experience attending the Vaccine Core Course at NMRTC San Diego when I was a junior Sailor,” Amponsah said. “The course changed my perspective on vaccines and immunizations.”

Amponsah said the combination of classroom education and practical training helped him develop skills that were not always covered during traditional Navy technical training. After completing the course, he was selected to assist as an instructor at NMRTC San Diego, an experience he said remained one of the most meaningful of his career as a hospital corpsman and preventive medicine technician.

When Amponsah reported to Twentynine Palms, he saw an opportunity to bring a similar training model to the command.

“Since checking in to NMRTC Twentynine Palms about two months ago, I have consistently heard Command Master Chief Richard Moreno emphasize the command’s commitment to professional development, patient safety, force health protection and warfighter readiness,” Amponsah said. “Those priorities reinforced my desire to bring this training to Twentynine Palms.”

Turning that idea into a commandwide training program required collaboration across multiple specialties and directorates. Public health leadership, immunization personnel, nurses, hospital corpsmen, staff education and training personnel and other subject-matter experts contributed to planning the course, developing instruction and staffing hands-on skills stations.

That broad support allowed the command to provide participants with training covering the vaccination process from the moment a patient arrives through vaccine administration and final documentation.

Classroom instruction covered vaccine fundamentals, influenza, patient screening, vaccine-administration routes, Vaccine Information Statements, clinical emergencies, risk communication and professionalism. Participants also learned health system documentation, vaccine adverse-event reporting, medical-waste disposal, needlestick protocols, cold-chain management and procedures for safely packing and transporting vaccines.

The practical portion of the course gave participants an opportunity to apply those lessons before demonstrating competency.

During skills stations, trainees practiced screening patients, preparing and administering vaccines, placing tuberculin skin tests, educating patients and responding to vaccine concerns. The training also covered recognizing conditions requiring referral to an onsite provider, managing anaphylaxis, administering epinephrine, responding to needlestick injuries and maintaining vaccines at appropriate temperatures.

Amponsah said developing those skills helps Sailors understand the entire vaccination process rather than focusing solely on administering an injection.

“Sailors learned and practiced the full vaccination workflow, from welcoming and screening patients to administering vaccines and documenting care,” he said.

Participants were required to complete a 25-question examination with a minimum passing score of 70% and demonstrate their skills through competency testing. Those who successfully completed the requirements received vaccinator competency validation and certificates of completion.

The inaugural class included personnel from nearly every area of the command, including medical services, public health, dental, surgical services, nursing services, clinical support services and administration.

While many participants were hospital corpsmen or other healthcare personnel, the class also included Sailors serving in nonmedical ratings, demonstrating an opportunity to broaden the command’s pool of trained personnel.

Operational medical personnel from 2nd Battalion, 7th Marines; 3rd Battalion, 7th Marines; and 3rd Battalion, 4th Marines also completed the training, extending its reach beyond the hospital and into units supporting Marines aboard Marine Corps Air-Ground Combat Center Twentynine Palms.

Amponsah said expanding the number of qualified vaccinators gives the command greater flexibility when responding to seasonal immunization efforts, periods of increased demand and other public health needs.

“This training is important because offering immunizations are a critical part of force health protection and operational medical readiness,” Amponsah said. “By developing a larger pool of qualified and competent vaccinators, NMRTC Twentynine Palms can provide timely immunization services, support seasonal vaccination efforts and respond more effectively during high-demand periods or public health events.”

That capability is particularly important in a military healthcare environment, where immunizations can help protect individual patients while also supporting the readiness of units preparing for training, deployments and operations.

Vaccine-preventable illnesses can affect the availability of service members and their ability to perform their missions. Maintaining a trained vaccinator workforce helps ensure offered immunizations can be delivered safely and efficiently while reducing the risk of disease non-battle injuries.

The course was also designed to standardize vaccination practices across the command by reinforcing current Defense Health Agency and Centers for Disease Control and Prevention guidance.

Beyond the technical skill of administering a vaccine, Amponsah said the training emphasized patient safety at every step, including screening for contraindications, educating patients, maintaining the vaccine cold chain and ensuring accurate documentation.

“The course also promotes consistent patient screening, safe vaccine administration, proper documentation and adherence to current clinical guidance,” Amponsah said. “These capabilities help protect service members, reduce the risk of vaccine-preventable illness and ensure Sailors are prepared to provide safe, reliable care whenever and wherever it is needed.”

With the first 34 graduates completing the course, the command is already looking toward making the training a sustained part of professional development at NMRTC Twentynine Palms.

The Basic Vaccinator Course is planned to be offered quarterly, allowing newly assigned personnel to receive training while helping the command maintain a larger pool of qualified vaccinators.

Amponsah also hopes future iterations will continue reaching personnel outside the hospital through collaboration with operational and Marine Corps medical units.

“The goal is for the Basic Vaccinator Course to become a recurring training opportunity at NMRTC Twentynine Palms,” Amponsah said. “Currently, the course will be offered quarterly to provide training for newly assigned personnel, sustain a qualified vaccinator workforce and maintain immunization competency across the command.”

For Amponsah, seeing the first class graduate represented the culmination of an effort that began with lessons he learned as a student years earlier and continued through the support of personnel throughout NMRTC Twentynine Palms.

“The success of the first Basic Vaccinator Course was truly a team effort,” Amponsah said. “I am proud of the 34 graduates and grateful to the command leadership, instructors, implementation team and support staff who helped make the course possible and a resounding success.”

More importantly, he said, the course gives Sailors another skill they can carry with them throughout Navy Medicine and into operational environments where their training may be needed.

“Most importantly, the course equips Sailors with the knowledge, practical skills and confidence they need to safely care for our patients and support the mission,” Amponsah said.

Navy Medicine Readiness and Training Command Twentynine Palms supports the readiness and health of service members, their families and other beneficiaries while maintaining a ready medical force capable of supporting operational requirements. The command includes Naval Hospital Twentynine Palms at Marine Corps Air-Ground Combat Center Twentynine Palms and branch health clinics at Naval Air Weapons Station China Lake and Marine Corps Mountain Warfare Training Center Bridgeport.

Navy Medicine’s 44,000-plus highly trained military and civilian healthcare professionals provide enduring expeditionary medical support to the warfighter on, below and above the sea, and ashore.

items.title: Protecting the Post: Alvarez Takes on Expanded Security Leadership
items.author: Courtesy
items.summary: Service members, families, civilian employees and community members gathered at the Directorate of Emergency Services, Oct. 1 to witness the promotion of Army civilian Police lieutenant Yoaliz Alvarez to captain, expanding her leadership role in the installation’s physical security mission.
items.body: FORT BUCHANAN, Puerto Rico — Service members, families, civilian employees and community members gathered at the Directorate of Emergency Services, Oct. 1 to witness the promotion of Army civilian Police lieutenant Yoaliz Alvarez to captain, expanding her leadership role in the installation’s physical security mission. Alvarez, who has served at the Army’s home in the Caribbean since 2022, now oversees approximately 30 personnel after previously supervising a team of 15 as a lieutenant. Her responsibilities include security operations at the Borinqueneers Gate and Spc. Frances M. Vega Gate, vehicle access operations and the Visitor Control Center. “This is a very big position, and I take it with that seriousness,” Alvarez said. “I’m honored and humbled to have this opportunity.” Thomas Acosta Lamberti, director of Fort Buchanan’s Directorate of Emergency Services, said Alvarez’s promotion supports the installation’s efforts to strengthen leadership and supervision within its Physical Security Section. “Captain Alvarez is highly qualified, and focused on the Buchanan mission and providing customer service to all our visitors, veterans and their dependents,” Acosta said. “She has the attributes that are required for the position, and she has the experience and the education to be a good physical security supervisor.” A resident of Carolina, Puerto Rico, Alvarez brings military, corrections and civilian law enforcement experience to the position. She enlisted in the Army in 2015 and served as a military police Soldier in security-related assignments before transitioning to civilian service. She also worked as a correctional officer at the Metropolitan Detention Center. Alvarez holds a bachelor’s degree in psychology from Inter American University of Puerto Rico. She said her education has helped her understand human behavior and communicate with the Soldiers, families, civilian employees, veterans and visitors her team serves. For Alvarez, working directly with people remains one of the most rewarding aspects of her job. “People. Being one-on-one with people,” Alvarez said when asked what she enjoys most about her work. “Let me see how I can help you, even if we can’t do specifically what you’re asking for.” That approach is especially important at the Visitor Control Center, where Alvarez and her team balance customer service with the responsibility of protecting the installation. As she assumes greater responsibility, Alvarez said her priorities remain focused on supporting her team, protecting the community and helping people navigate installation access requirements. For information about installation access, contact the Fort Buchanan Visitor Control Center at the Borinqueneers Gate at 787-707-3995. To stay informed about the latest updates at Fort Buchanan, the community is encouraged to download the MAPA app on their mobile devices, select Fort Buchanan as their installation, and enable notifications. Fort Buchanan supports approximately 15,000 military personnel, including active-duty Soldiers, Army Reserve, Puerto Rico National Guard, Marine Corps Reserve and Navy Reserve members. The installation’s mission is to enable readiness and facilitate the deployment of forces anytime, anywhere.

items.title: WAMC, Naval Medical Center Camp Lejeune Advance Regional Medical Readiness
items.author: Keisha Frith
items.summary: Leaders from Womack Army Medical Center (WAMC) and Naval Medical Center Camp Lejeune (NMCCL) recently met to welcome newly assigned leaders, exchange best practices and reinforce a shared commitment to proactive collaboration across the region in support of the Joint Force. The engagement focused on strengthening inter-service communication, aligning operational capabilities and identifying opportunities to improve efficiency and problem-solving within the military health enterprise.
items.body:
FORT BRAGG, N.C. --Leaders from Womack Army Medical Center (WAMC) and Naval Medical Center Camp Lejeune (NMCCL) recently met to welcome newly assigned leaders, exchange best practices and reinforce a shared commitment to proactive collaboration across the region in support of the Joint Force. The engagement focused on strengthening inter-service communication, aligning operational capabilities and identifying opportunities to improve efficiency and problem-solving within the military health enterprise. Our focus is on building deliberate, collaborative relationships that enhance readiness and improve how we care for those we serve,” said Col. Kane Morgan, WAMC commander. “Working closely with our partners across the region ensures our Soldiers, families and beneficiaries receive the highest quality medical support.”

The visit provided WAMC and NMCCL leaders an opportunity to strengthen coordination, exchange best practices and identify ways to improve joint medical readiness across the region.

“The primary purpose of this engagement is to forge actionable, joint-force partnerships that directly enhance regional medical readiness,” said Capt. Kathryn M. Stewart, commander and director, Naval Medical Center Camp Lejeune. “At NMCCL, our priority is ensuring our medical personnel and operational forces are prepared to meet strategic demands.”

Stewart said close collaboration between NMCCL and WAMC enables the organizations to share best practices, streamline clinical pathways and optimize resources across service branches.

“Both medical centers service significant patient volumes and critical trauma missions,” Stewart said. “By unifying our efforts, we boost regional healthcare capacity and ensure our service members, whether they be Marine Corps, Navy or Army, are fully supported and medically mission ready.”

During the discussion, both command teams emphasized the importance of transparency, early coordination and leveraging organizational strengths to address challenges at the lowest level. Leaders also highlighted ongoing initiatives that may be adaptable across departments to enhance joint readiness and improve health service delivery. Following the meeting, the NMCCL) command team toured the Emergency Department and Labor and Delivery units and met with Operating Room leadership and staff to gain a deeper understanding of WAMC’s operational capabilities and current clinical workflows. Leaders engaged directly with staff, asked questions and identified shared priorities in joint mission requirements. The visit also provided visibility into practices currently in use at one facility that may support efficiency or continuous improvement efforts at the other.

Looking ahead, Stewart said NMCCL views the partnership as a unified commitment to warfighter readiness. The commands plan to explore opportunities to integrate and leverage strengths across mental health care networks, vital blood supply chains, and academic and clinical research advancements.

The engagement reinforced a unified commitment to collaboration, continuous improvement and delivering high-quality support to Soldiers, Sailors, Marines, families and beneficiaries across the region.

items.title: Don’t be a target of scams about TRICARE
items.author: Courtesy
items.summary: If you’ve gotten a suspicious phone call or message about your TRICARE coverage, don’t respond to it. Instead, report it to TRICARE.
items.body:
If you’ve gotten a suspicious phone call or message about your TRICARE coverage, don’t respond to it. Instead, report it to TRICARE .

There are many types of phishing scams targeted toward the military community, as described by Military OneSource . Beneficiaries may get calls, messages, emails, or texts from scammers claiming to be with TRICARE.

“Scammers may try to target anyone with TRICARE coverage,” said Kathy McGuire, Chief, Managed Care Support Branch, TRICARE Health Plan, at the Defense Health Agency. “Stay aware and report any suspicious calls or messages that say they’re from TRICARE.”

It’s important to know that TRICARE or its contractors won’t call you to collect payment or offer discounts. TRICARE will never text or call you asking for:

Personal identifying information (such as your Social Security number, date of birth, or DOD ID number)

Keep these tips in mind when it comes to your personal information:

Never share personal or financial information with someone you don’t know.

Don’t open unsolicited, unexpected text messages or emails.

Don’t open links from unknown numbers or emails. Instead, contact your TRICARE contractor using a phone number or website you know is real to verify that they’re trying to reach you.

Ensure your contact information remains current with TRICARE to avoid your personal data from being breached. Personal data may be sent via mail or email to unintended recipients if your contact information isn’t kept up to date.

Have you or someone you know gotten a scam phone call, text, email, or letter? You should report any suspected fraud or abuse related to your TRICARE benefits.

There are two ways to make a report :

Option 1: Contact your TRICARE contractor . Depending on your plan, this may be your regional contractor, the TRICARE For Life contractor, the pharmacy contractor, or the TRICARE Dental Program contractor.

Option 2: Contact the DHA Office of the Inspector General .

Give as much information as possible when you make your report. This may include names, dates, and details. Investigations are confidential. You can choose to remain anonymous.

Protect your personal information. Treat it like a credit card. If someone contacts you by phone, email, or text message asking for this information, don’t provide it. Instead, report it to your TRICARE contractor right away.

Preventing TRICARE fraud and abuse is everyone’s responsibility. To learn more about how to spot scams, check out the FBI’s tips on catching healthcare fraud .

items.title: It’s official: US Army’s improved M8 rifle to begin fielding in December
items.author: Hope Hodge Seck
items.summary: The U.S. Army will begin fielding Sig Sauer’s M8 rifle in December, replacing the M7 with a lighter, shorter carbine based on soldier feedback.
items.body:
NEWINGTON, N.H. – On the factory floor at gun maker Sig Sauer’s headquarters, giant shipping pallets of the brand-new M8 Next Generation Squad Weapon rifle sit shrink-wrapped on shelves, ready for dispatch to soldiers.

Fielding of the M8 carbine, which appears set to replace Sig Sauer’s M7 as the Army’s standard rifle less than three years after the M7’s initial fielding began, will begin in December with some units at Fort Bragg, North Carolina, company executives confirmed to Military Times Monday.

The NGSW new weapons rollout also includes Sig’s M250 machine gun, which will replace the aging M249 Squad Automatic Weapon and is expected to reach troops in the first half of next year, said Dave Buehler, the company’s vice president of manufacturing.

Both weapons share an ammunition caliber: the 6.8×51mm Common Cartridge developed by Sig Sauer with a hybrid design intended to withstand high chamber pressure.

The M7 stumbled out of the gate, generating complaints from soldiers about its unwieldy weight and length and undue wear they said the high-pressure rounds were putting on components, including barrels and suppressors.

While Sig Sauer pushed back at the time on a number of the most strident complaints, the company is now casting the transition from the M7 to the M8, also previously called the XM8, as a success story that highlights its ability to act quickly on soldier inputs.

“From our perspective [the M8 is] a far superior rifle to the M7,” Buehler said. “On the M7, our hands were kind of tied [with what] the design criteria or characteristics of the contract required – even if we didn’t like them, we had to meet them. So now, the M8 considers our feedback, the soldiers’ feedback. And we can’t wait to get it out there.”

The new rifle is more than a pound lighter than the M7 and sports a barrel that’s 3.5 inches shorter. It replaces a less-popular folding stock with a fixed stock and includes feedback-based adjustments like added rigidity for the handguard. For soldiers who previously received the M7 rifle, the M8 should be a smooth transition, said Josh Shoemaker, Sig Sauer’s product manager for defense.

“The fundamentals are all the same, really,” Shoemaker told Military Times in an interview. “If guys that have had the M7 already are pretty familiar with that, the M8 will be a well-received transition.”

The foremost design challenge, he said, was achieving weight reduction from the M7, which weighed more than eight pounds unloaded, and nearly 10 pounds with the included suppressor – a radical difference from the legacy M4A1 carbine, which weighs 6.34 pounds unloaded.

Shoemaker said Sig Sauer had reduced the weight difference between the M4 and M8 to a little less than a pound, though that doesn’t include the M8’s suppressor.

“We worked really hard to reduce weight where we could and where it matters. So there’s lots of lightening cuts around the receiver. We pulled some weight out of the barrel, but we’re very careful to do that, because a lot of times when you pull weight out of the barrel, you have risks of some performance decreasing, whether that be barrel life or cook-off,” Shoemaker said. “We’re very sensitive to that, so it’s a long process to be able to figure out where your left and right limit is and how much weight [you can] kind of pull off of that before it’s too much.”

Reducing barrel size and thus altering the weapon’s center of gravity helped in that effort, Shoemaker said.

“When you pick up that M8, the balance of it feels a lot better, with that suppressor being on a shorter weapon system,” he added.

As for the M7, budget documents released earlier this year show the Army is curtailing its procurement, with none additional requested for Fiscal Year 2027 and about 50,000 previously delivered to the force.

The Army hasn’t said what it plans to do with the M7s already in inventory, particularly if it opts to put M8s in the hands of all troops who previously got the M7.

Shoemaker said there were “tons of options” for the Army with regard to M7s, including sending the weapons to basic training units or reassigning them to Guard or Reserve units.

But there’s another option, he said: the Army could ask for conversion kits to turn all the M7s already in its inventory into M8 carbines.

“The barrel is two screws that come out, and the hand guard is two more screws … the lower-end serialized item is the same,” he said. “All in, you could probably convert [an M7 to an M8] in under five minutes.”

If that’s an option Army leaders are considering, they have yet to address it publicly.

“There’re lots of options that the Army is well aware of,” Shoemaker said, “and making decisions on what direction they’ll go with that.”
