items.title: Six Scottish soldiers buried in France 108 years after their deaths
items.summary: MOD War Detectives used DNA evidence to identify two of the fallen, four remain unknown though one was identified as having served with the Argyll & Sutherland Highlanders whilst the other three likely served with the Gordon Highlanders.
items.body:
Relatives gathered in France today to witness the burial with full military honours of two Scottish soldiers of World War 1 and four of their unknown comrades.

Private ( Pte ) George Fleming Brock and Pte Percy Todd, both 11th Battalion, Argyll & Sutherland Highlanders, were laid to rest alongside four unknown soldiers 108 years after they were killed in action during the German Spring Offensive in 1918.

Pte Brock of Dunipace, West Falkirk, was serving an architectural apprenticeship with the Stirling firm of Messrs Bruce & Livingston when he enlisted in June 1916. Only a month after joining the Argyll & Sutherland Highlanders in France, he was seriously wounded by gunshot and spent several months recuperating in hospital.

He rejoined the battalion in January 1918. Two months later the Germans launched a huge offensive on the Western Front. On 28 March 1918, Pte Brock’s battalion were holding positions in the area of Tilloy-les-Mofflaines, when they were overwhelmed by intense bombardment. It was on this day that Private Brock lost his life, aged just 19.

Pte Todd of Radford, Nottinghamshire, was a draper’s manager at Bryan’s Drapery in Isleworth, London, when he enlisted in November 1915. He was living with his wife, Alice, who he had met eight years earlier at work. Pte Todd was also seriously wounded shortly after joining the battalion, on the first day of the Battle of Arras in 1917. After a long recovery, he rejoined his battalion in February 1918, but lost his life less than two months later during the German Spring Offensive, on 5 April 1918.

In 2023, during an archaeological survey on a site in Tilloy-les-Mofflaines the six men were recovered. Found with them were a variety of artefacts, including regimental insignia from the Argyll & Sutherland Highlanders, and from the Gordon Highlanders. After extensive historical research and DNA testing, two of these casualties were identified as Private Brock and Private Todd. The two men were buried alongside four others who could not be identified.

The service was organised by the MOD ’s Joint Casualty and Compassionate Centre ( JCCC ), also known as the ‘ MOD War Detectives’ who work to identify the recovered remains of British military casualties.

Nicola Nash, MOD War Detective said:

Private Brock and Private Todd have both been buried today 108 years after they were killed. With half a million British servicemen still missing from World War 1, every identity we make is a huge achievement. It has been a real privilege to give closure to their families and lay these heroes to rest with honour.

David Royle, Recoveries and Ceremonies Manager at CWGC , said:

For 108 years, these six men lay where they fell on the battlefield. It is a privilege and a source of great pride for the CWGC to have recovered them and worked alongside the JCCC in the effort to restore their identities. While four of these soldiers sadly remain unidentified, they are not forgotten. We will care for their graves, and for those of Private Todd and Private Brock, in perpetuity, ensuring that future generations have opportunity to honour and remember their sacrifice.

items.title: Graves of five soldiers killed in Normandy identified
items.summary: Five missing soldiers of World War 2 who were killed during the Battle of Normandy now have named graves after Rededication ceremonies were held on 29 and 30 September 26, and 1 October 26.
items.body:
The graves of five soldiers who went missing during the Battle of Normandy have been identified and were rededicated this week. A commemorative service honouring all five men, was also held at the British Normandy Memorial in Ver-sur-Mer (30 September 26).

Rededication services took place at CWGC St Charles-de-Percy War Cemetery for Private ( Pte ) George Chapman of 1st Battalion The Herefordshire Regiment (29 September 26), at CWGC Bayeux War Cemetery for Private Vincent Coia of 7th Battalion The Seaforth Highlanders and Lance Corporal ( LCpl ) Reginald Cyril Dewey of 4th Battalion The Lincolnshire Regiment (30 September 26), at CWGC Hottot-les-Bagues War Cemetery for Serjeant ( Sjt ) Frederick Albert Harrison of 1st Battalion The Dorsetshire Regiment and at CWGC Ranville War Cemetery for Corporal ( Cpl ) Henry Thomas Read of 8th Battalion The Rifle Brigade (1 October 26).

Members of the Chapman, Dewey and Read families were present at their relatives’ rededication service. The Coia and Harrison families were not able to attend, but a poignant message from Reg Harrison, the 95 year old younger brother of Sjt Harrison, was read out at his graveside in Hottot-les-Bagues War Cemetery.

Although I didn’t know my brother very well, as I was only young when he left home to join the army, I’m very proud of him and what he achieved, and what he went onto do for his King and country. It was soldiers like Fred that helped us win the war, and keep us safe. Always in my thoughts. Your young brother, Reg.

The services were organised by the Ministry of Defence’s Joint Casualty and Compassionate Centre ( JCCC ), known as the ‘War Detectives’, and were supported by serving soldiers from 5th Battalion The Rifles, 2nd Battalion The Royal Anglian Regiment and 2nd Battalion The Royal Regiment of Scotland.

Rosie Barron, JCCC Caseworker, said:

It has been an honour to have organised these rededication services and to have played a part in giving these families answers as to what happened to their relatives. The local community in Normandy has been very welcoming of both the families and the military party. For them the Battle of Normandy is not just commemorated but celebrated as the moment that they regained their liberty after four long years of occupation. The sacrifices made by these men were not in vain. There are many graves in Normandy which may yet be identifiable with further investigation, so this work will continue into the future.

Reverend Paul Collins CF, Chaplain to 5th Battalion The Rifles, conducted the services.

Reverend Paul Collins said:

It is my privilege to be able part of these rededication services. These brave soldiers gave their lives in the events following D-Day which led to the liberation of France and the defeat of the Nazis. It is fitting that due to the hard work of the JCCC Commemorations Team and others, we now know who these soldiers were and where they are buried. The graves now bear their names for all those who visit in the future to see and remember.

All five men had previously been commemorated on the Bayeux Memorial to the missing. The CWGC has now replaced their headstones with named markers and will care for them in perpetuity.

Dr James Wallis, Head of Commemorations at the CWGC , said:

The Commission’s staff consider it a privilege to care for the now-identified graves of these five soldiers who were killed in the aftermath of D-Day during the Battle of Normandy. The impact of loss upon the respective families of these casualties still resonates strongly – so we are thankful to those who instigated each identification and furthermore to the work of partner organisations which has led to this outcome and brought us together today.

items.title: 30% boost to UK military transport aircraft availability under new deal
items.summary: MoD extends £190 million contract with Airbus to maintain the RAF's A400M Atlas fleet, boosting aircraft availability while sustaining over 350 UK jobs.
items.body:
£190 million contract extension with Airbus to support RAF’s A400 Atlas fleet, retaining more than 350 UK jobs.

Agreement set to increase the number of mission-capable A400M aircraft available each day from 10 to 13 by the end of 2027.

Britain’s air defence will be boosted under new deal.

A 30% improvement in availability for the RAF’s tactical and strategic airlift fleet will be delivered under a £190 million contract extension between the Ministry of Defence and Airbus.

The extension will see Airbus continue its maintenance, repair and support services for the RAF’s A400M Atlas fleet from its UK Support Centre at RAF Brize Norton.

As well as sustaining more than 350 UK jobs, the extended contract is set to deliver a significant boost to operational capability and will increase the number of fully mission-capable aircraft available each day from 10 to 13 by the end of 2027.

Minister for Defence Readiness and Industry, Luke Pollard MP said:

This contract extension is a vote of confidence in British engineering, and the workforce at Brize Norton and Carterton who keep our A400M fleet flying. By boosting availability of these aircraft, we’re strengthening the RAF’s ability to conduct global operations and deliver on NATO commitments when it matters most, while backing UK jobs and delivering value for money for taxpayers.

This contract extension is a vote of confidence in British engineering, and the workforce at Brize Norton and Carterton who keep our A400M fleet flying.

By boosting availability of these aircraft, we’re strengthening the RAF’s ability to conduct global operations and deliver on NATO commitments when it matters most, while backing UK jobs and delivering value for money for taxpayers.

The A400M Atlas is a cornerstone of the UK’s air mobility capability, supporting operations ranging from humanitarian relief to rapid troop deployment.

Continued support at RAF Brize Norton ensures the fleet remains ready to meet these demands without interruption, forming part of the government’s wider commitment to strengthening the UK’s defence industrial base and value for money in defence contracts.

Air Cdre Si Young, Head Air Mobility in National Armaments Materiel, said:

This contract will deliver continued improvements in A400M fleet availability, building on the growth that we have delivered over recent years and giving our Armed Forces the capability they need while offering excellent value for money to taxpayers, supporting a platform that is at the heart of the RAF’s operations now and into the future. It reflects the strength of our partnership with Airbus and our shared commitment to supporting the continued growth and success of the A400M fleet, both now and in the years ahead.

This contract will deliver continued improvements in A400M fleet availability, building on the growth that we have delivered over recent years and giving our Armed Forces the capability they need while offering excellent value for money to taxpayers, supporting a platform that is at the heart of the RAF’s operations now and into the future.

It reflects the strength of our partnership with Airbus and our shared commitment to supporting the continued growth and success of the A400M fleet, both now and in the years ahead.

The 31-month extension to the Medium-Term Contract means support services will continue until April 2029, sustaining more than 240 Airbus staff and 110 primary sub-contract staff.

Kata Escott, Managing Director of Airbus Defence and Space UK, said:

Airbus is proud to be a trusted partner to the Ministry of Defence, and this contract extension reinforces that commitment. The A400M Atlas is the backbone of Air Mobility. Our highly skilled teams work side by side with Royal Air Force personnel and are fully focused on enhancing operational readiness, keeping the fleet mission-ready.

The contract builds on the work of the Defence Investment Plan, which commits £298 billion to UK defence over the next four years. The plan will drive sustained investment across British industry ensuring the UK’s defence sector remains a cornerstone of the country’s economic renewal.

items.title: Sexual Assault and Sexual Harassment in the Coast Guard
items.author: Sarah Weilant
items.summary: The authors evaluate the Coast Guard’s sexual assault and sexual harassment prevention and response strategies, victim support services to support recovery efforts, and accountability mechanisms.
items.body:
Holistic Study and Analysis

ResearchPublished Oct 2, 2026

This research was conducted within HSOAC, a federally funded research and development center operated by RAND under contract with DHS.

Sexual assault and sexual harassment (SASH) threaten the safety, trust, and cohesion essential to mission readiness in the U.S. Coast Guard. The authors evaluate the Coast Guard’s SASH prevention and response strategies, victim support services to support recovery efforts, and accountability mechanisms.

Sexual assault and sexual harassment (SASH) threaten the safety, trust, and cohesion essential to mission readiness in the U.S. Coast Guard. Investigations, internal reviews, and high-profile reports have highlighted systemic challenges in how the service prevents, responds to, and accounts for these behaviors.

In response, Congress directed the U.S. Department of Homeland Security to commission an independent review of the Coast Guard’s approach to SASH. The authors conducted this study to provide an impartial, evidence-informed assessment of the service’s policies, programs, and institutional practices related to SASH. Separately, the Coast Guard conducted its own Accountability and Transparency Review, commissioned by the Commandant in July 2023, which produced 33 recommended actions to address harmful behaviors and strengthen accountability across the service. The authors examine Coast Guard efforts in light of those findings and recommendations while also identifying areas of progress, persistent gaps, and opportunities for structural improvement.

The purpose of the overall project is to evaluate the Coast Guard’s prevention and response strategies, victim support services to support recovery efforts, and accountability mechanisms for SASH. The authors assess the Coast Guard’s policies, how responsibilities are distributed across programs, and how requirements are executed in practice across a geographically dispersed workforce. Particular attention is given to transparency, command involvement, and the extent to which current systems prevent sexual assault and harassment and support both survivor needs and institutional accountability.

- The Coast Guard’s SASH efforts are constrained less by an absence of programs than by how those programs are structured, integrated, and resourced.

- The most foundational concerns involve fragmented policy architecture and data. SASH-related policy is distributed across three distinct directives, with no single integrating framework.

- Data on SASH incidents are similarly fragmented across multiple tracking systems with differing definitions and reporting standards, which limits the Coast Guard’s ability to assess trends, evaluate what is working, and identify where risk is concentrated.

- Prevention and leadership present related challenges. The Coast Guard’s prevention activity is largely training-centric, with success measured by course completion rates rather than demonstrated changes in behavior or risk.

- The response and support system faces ongoing challenges. Survivors and stakeholders expressed continued concern about long investigative timelines, limited visibility into case status, and inconsistent communication.

- Quantitatively, official sexual assault reporting rates have been relatively stable in recent years, but survey-based estimates of prevalence consistently exceed official report counts, indicating that underreporting remains a significant concern.

- Fragmented policy architecture limits coherence, clarity of authority, and accountability. One option would be to establish a single authoritative instruction consolidating SASH prevention, response, recovery, and accountability; another would retain the existing program-specific instructions while introducing a formal governance body to coordinate them and track implementation.

- Prevention is treated primarily as training compliance rather than as a sustained capability. One option would reframe prevention as an enterprise capability with measurable outcome targets; another would require individual programs to articulate how their activities reduce risk.

- Variable training quality, consistency, and focus limit prevention effectiveness. One option would establish a tiered model based on unit risk; another would build risk-based triggers into existing policy.

- Commanders are expected to foster safe and accountable unit climates, but policy provides limited behavioral specificity and no structured accountability mechanisms. One option is to articulate specific behavioral expectations for leaders in policy and to reinforce those expectations through professional development and evaluation.

- Response systems have improved, but trust remains fragile due to communication, transparency, and timeline challenges. One option is to standardize communication practices across the response system; another would focus on reducing investigative timelines through process improvements.

- Resource constraints create a reactive system with limited capacity for prevention and sustained engagement. One option would assign new billets or assignments based on risk and geographic access; another would expand capacity through augmentation strategies.

- Data fragmentation and governance challenges limit evaluation, oversight, and organizational learning. One option would move toward an integrated data environment; another would clarify data stewardship and improve interoperability across existing systems.

items.title: AI Data Center Siting on Federal Lands
items.author: Jennifer Buckley
items.summary: The U.S. government is opening federal land for data center development. In this report, the authors explore how the government could facilitate the siting and construction of data centers on federal land within the context of energy constraints.
items.body:
A new RAND data center siting rubric helps federal agencies screen and rank potential sites based on energy feasibility.

The U.S. government, spurred by a 2025 executive order, is moving quickly to open federal land for artificial intelligence (AI) data center development and directing agencies to identify suitable sites. But energy availability—not just available acreage—is a binding constraint that will determine which sites can realistically support large-scale AI infrastructure.

RAND researchers evaluated 12 U.S. Department of War sites offered for data center leases, compared them with 17 U.S. Department of Energy sites, and developed a cost model to estimate energy infrastructure expenses across 31 candidate locations. A stakeholder workshop stress-tested these findings and informed public-private partnership guidance.

Most sites will require major energy investment.

- Across both departments, nearly every candidate site lacks sufficient existing generation capacity to power a gigawatt-scale data center without significant new infrastructure.

Site rankings shift depending on scale and financing.

- No single site dominates under all conditions. Sites in the southwest perform best for most scenarios, while several northeastern sites consistently rank at the bottom.

Energy costs rival facility construction costs.

- At the gigawatt scale, energy infrastructure expenses are comparable in magnitude to data center construction costs, making energy planning a primary—not secondary—driver of site selection.

Unresolved conflicts can become national security risks.

- A workshop exercise found that community opposition, litigation, and infrastructure disputes at a federally approved data center site could escalate into overlapping legal, political, and security crises that threaten development.

When screening potential sites for development:

- Use a site-screening framework that ranks candidates on energy costs, grid interconnection feasibility, and infrastructure readiness before solicitations are issued.

- Request that bidders describe how they will meet the Ratepayer Protection Pledge—the commitment that data center energy costs will not raise electricity rates for consumers.

- Treat energy infrastructure as a parallel, coequal workstream alongside civil construction in all requests for lease proposals rather than as a subordinate component to be resolved after a lease has been awarded.

When enabling public-private partnerships:

- Develop formal policy guidelines for data center public-private partnerships covering site-specific engagement, risk allocation, security responsibilities, and decommissioning obligations.

RAND researchers applied a previously developed energy suitability framework covering energy supply, energy systems, supporting inputs, environmental conditions, and governance factors to 12 U.S. Department of War sites. They then developed a quantitative energy cost model to estimate the present-value cost of powering a 1-gigawatt data center across 31 candidate sites using four generation scenarios. Sensitivity analyses tested how rankings change under varying assumptions about compute scale, the cost of capital, and cooling requirements. A structured stakeholder workshop with 14 federal and industry participants, including a scenario-based Day After exercise, generated inputs for public-private partnership guidance.

items.title: UK leads major Joint Expeditionary Force Exercise as defence ministers meet in Iceland
items.summary: The UK is ramping up its defence of the High North and Baltic to combat Russian hybrid threats with the Joint Expeditionary Force conducting major exercises across the region.
items.body:
Hundreds of British personnel train with allies from the UK-led Joint Expeditionary Force (JEF) to counter rising Russian threat in Exercise Lion Protector 26.

Training takes place across the North Atlantic, High North, and Baltic Sea, with Royal Marines conducting the first exercise in the Faroe Islands since the Second World War.

Comes as the Defence Secretary meets JEF counterparts in Iceland, with Canada and Ukraine also in attendance.

The UK is ramping up its defence of the High North and Baltic to combat Russian hybrid threats with the Joint Expeditionary Force conducting major exercises across the region.

Allies from the Joint Expeditionary Force (JEF), which is led by the UK, have conducted Exercise Lion Protector 26, which saw forces train across the North Atlantic, High North, and Baltic Sea to protect critical national infrastructure, strengthen joint command and control, and counter emerging threats.

From the data cables that connect the UK to the world, to the energy infrastructure that powers homes and businesses, the North Atlantic and High North are vital to our national security.

It comes as the Defence Secretary today meets with his JEF counterparts at a summit in Keflavik, Iceland, where ministers will progress discussions on Canada’s application for membership of the JEF Framework.

Ministers will also discuss deepening cooperation on countering hybrid threats, furthering industrial collaboration, and support to Ukraine through the JEF-Ukraine Enhanced Partnership. As Canada and Ukraine continue to cooperate closely with JEF, Canadian and Ukrainian ministers will also be in attendance.

Part of Exercise Lion Protector 26 saw Royal Marines from the UK’s Special Operations Maritime Task Group conduct the first exercise since the Second World War on the Faroe Islands, alongside Danish forces.

Marines and their Danish allies carried out maritime interdictions, amphibious landings, and vertical ascent training on the Faroes, which was the location of a key Royal Marines deployment during the Second World War.

Defence Secretary Wes Streeting MP said:

The North Atlantic, High North, and Baltic are the frontline of the UK’s security, which is why British leadership of the Joint Expeditionary Force is so vital to our defence. From conducting amphibious landings on the Faroe Islands, to deploying a standing headquarters north of the Arctic Circle, our recent JEF exercises have shown how Britain is working with our allies to enhance NATO’s defence of the region in the face of rising Russian threats. I was also delighted that we welcomed our Canadian and Ukrainian counterparts to the summit as JEF seeks to expand its cooperation with these crucial allies.

The North Atlantic, High North, and Baltic are the frontline of the UK’s security, which is why British leadership of the Joint Expeditionary Force is so vital to our defence.

From conducting amphibious landings on the Faroe Islands, to deploying a standing headquarters north of the Arctic Circle, our recent JEF exercises have shown how Britain is working with our allies to enhance NATO’s defence of the region in the face of rising Russian threats.

I was also delighted that we welcomed our Canadian and Ukrainian counterparts to the summit as JEF seeks to expand its cooperation with these crucial allies.

Lion Protector launched in August with a rehearsal of a multi-national maritime escort operation stretching the length of the Baltic Sea. Warships and aircraft from Denmark, Latvia, Sweden and the UK escorted a Danish vessel carrying military equipment to Latvia, testing the JEF’s ability to coordinate rapidly across sea, land, air, cyber and space.

The UK’s Standing Joint Force Headquarters coordinated activity across the High North and Baltic Sea region, deploying north of the Arctic Circle in Norway to test its ability to command allied forces at speed and range.

JEF is a UK-led coalition of ten like-minded nations comprising high readiness forces configured to respond rapidly to crises in support of NATO security. JEF brings together the UK, Denmark, Estonia, Finland, Iceland, Latvia, Lithuania, the Netherlands, Norway and Sweden to secure the Baltic Sea, North Atlantic, Arctic and High North for NATO.

Today’s summit builds on the JEF Leaders’ Summit in Helsinki in March where leaders agreed to reinforce steadfast support to Ukraine through ambitious delivery of the JEF-Ukraine Enhanced Partnership.

It also builds on the Prime Minister’s discussions with Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Støre this week about the hybrid threat Russia poses.

Exercise Lion Protector 26 comes ahead of the Atlantic Future Forum and the International Sea Power Conference, both taking place in Oslo in November.

items.title: 9/11's Forgotten Lesson
items.summary: Twenty-five years later, 9/11's lessons are still contested, except the simplest: the United States mistook quiet for peace. And it is doing so again.
items.body:
On a sunny, crisp early-fall New England morning, I strolled across the leafy central quad in the middle of campus. I had to register for classes in person, and to avoid the crowds, I got there right as the doors opened. After completing that task, I met a friend and fellow cadet setting up the Reserve Officer Training Corps recruiting booth for a student activity fair later that day. He's the person who told me that a plane had just hit the World Trade Center. I rushed back to my dorm and unpacked my television. As I saw the video of the planes hitting the towers, I knew that I was going to war.

A quarter century after the most significant attack on American soil since Pearl Harbor, the national security lessons from 9/11 are still unsettled—a debate that has defined much of my professional life.

But to me, the lesson from 9/11 that I worry we overlook is simple: the perils of mistaking quiet for peace.

The failure to identify and stop the 9/11 terrorist attacks triggered a wave of internal institutional reforms in the United States. Believing that the intelligence community failed to connect the dots, Congress created the Office of the Director of National Intelligence to encourage greater information sharing. It also created the Department of Homeland Security to counter terrorist threats and the Transportation Security Administration to make the government—not private companies—responsible for airport security.

The rationale behind these new entities is no longer accepted wisdom, however. Some in the Trump administration have questioned the utility of an additional layer of management in the Office of the Director of National Intelligence and moved to dramatically downsize it. Others have questioned the costs of TSA and proposed reprivatizing security in smaller airports. Some Democrats have proposed dismantling the Department of Homeland Security as debates about the department's role in immigration enforcement have heated up.

Unsurprisingly, 9/11 also touched off a vigorous debate over what we should have learned about American posture in the Middle East, the utility of regime change as a strategy, and the United States' role in the world. There is even less consensus about these grander questions.

For some, the central lesson of the Global War on Terrorism's $8 trillion price tag and 900,000 casualties is that the United States needs to avoid such wars in the first place. In practice, that means restraining U.S. ambitions and constraining its ability to fight. And yet, even after the formal ends of the Iraq and Afghanistan wars, and despite sporadic attempts to repeal it over the years, the blanket Congressional authorization for the use of force that opened the door to military action after 9/11 remains in place. The United States hasn't withdrawn from the Middle East either, because the region's problems—and the reasons the country has remained actively engaged there—persist.

Finally, as problematic as regime change is as a strategy, it's not always clear what the alternative is. Even after the Iraq and Afghanistan wars, every successive American administration—both Republican and Democrat—has called for regime change somewhere in the world—whether in Libya, Syria, Russia, Venezuela, or Iran.

The most straightforward and least contentious lesson of 9/11 is also the one that gets the least attention: the price of complacency. After all, 9/11 was not a true bolt out of the blue. The United States had been tracking Osama bin Laden. It knew that al Qaeda had attacked the Americans in Africa and the Middle East with ever greater lethality. It even experienced an attack, albeit on a smaller scale, on the eventual target of 9/11 hijackers—the World Trade Center. At that point, though, the United States could not fathom that al Qaeda could strike with such ferocity that it would upend the comparatively benign environment of the post-Cold War world. The United States paid a terrible price for mistaking serenity for security.

The United States paid a terrible price for mistaking serenity for security.

The United States risks a similar error today. After all, the United States has talked openly about the growing threat from the same list of foreign adversaries—China, Russia, Iran, North Korea, and violent nonstate actors—since the Obama administration. Multiple experts from both inside (PDF) and outside of government over a period of more than a decade have raised the alarm about the growing threat of major war. The United States has glimpsed what the future of war holds in Ukraine and now Iran.

Despite these increasingly dire warnings, the United States remains woefully underprepared. China dwarfs the United States in shipbuilding. Wars in Ukraine and the Middle East have strained the American supplies of key munitions. The Iran War underscored the vulnerability of fixed bases on land and the logistical challenges of protracted operations at sea. And the United States finds itself struggling to adapt its military to technologies—from drones to artificial intelligence—that are upending modern warfare.

The drumbeats are growing louder. In the Middle East, both China and Russia have increased support for Iran as the war has dragged on. In Europe, Russia has targeted NATO allies as its military fortunes in Ukraine have stalled, with potentially even more aggressive moves yet to come. And in Asia, China continues its military build-up and has stepped up its drills to potentially blockade Taiwan. Any one of these situations, if mishandled, is enough to spark not just another Global War on Terrorism, but a global war more akin to those of the first half of the 20th century rather than the first decade of the 21st, full stop.

Reading the headlines coming out of Washington these days, you wouldn't know that the United States and the world at large sit on such a precipice. We are more comfortable continuing to debate the other unresolved lessons of 9/11 than face the one right in front of us.

We are still that proverbial college student strolling through the quad enjoying the lovely fall day.

items.title: USecAF sees Ramstein AB Airmen, Guardian readiness firsthand
items.author: First Lt. Jacob Willoughby
items.summary: The visit provided an opportunity for Lohmeier to meet with command leaders and subject matter experts, who offered insights on current and future missions, challenges and opportunities.
items.body:
Published Oct. 1, 2026

By First Lt. Jacob Willoughby

U.S. Air Forces in Europe - Air Forces Africa Public Affairs

Under Secretary of the Air Force Matt Lohmeier visited with U.S. Air Forces Europe-Air Forces Africa and U.S. Space Forces in Europe and Space Forces Africa leadership, Airmen and Guardians during an immersion visit at Ramstein Air Base, Sept. 24. The visit, which included stops at the USAFE-AFAFRICA headquarters, SPACEFOREUR-AF headquarters, 86th Airlift Wing, 603rd Air Operations Center, and 435th Air Ground Operations Wing, provided an opportunity for Lohmeier to meet with command leaders and subject matter experts, who offered insights on current and future missions, challenges and opportunities. “It’s a true privilege to visit Ramstein and see firsthand all the critical missions they execute in support of our warfighters,” Lohmeier said. “The motivation, service and expertise they display give me confidence our warfighters are ready to fight and win. We, as senior leaders, need to ensure they receive the most technologically advanced capabilities to execute their mission.” He started the day off with a workout session with SPACEFOREUR-AF Guardians and leadership, reinforcing that maintaining physical standards helps ensure military members are resilient and ready for anything the service demands of them. “Fitness is part of readiness, and leaders have to set that example,” Lohmeier said. “Whether you are at home station, deployed or on the road, taking care of yourself physically helps ensure you are prepared to lead and accomplish the mission.” Then Lohmeier received briefings on command missions and current operations. He spoke with U.S. Air Force Lt. Gen. Jason T. Hinds , USAFE-AFAFRICA commander, to discuss how the command defends the strategic approaches to the United States and generates airpower across two continents in support of U.S. European Command and U.S. Africa Command. “It was extremely valuable to meet with General Hinds to discuss how USAFE-AFAFAFRICA protects the U.S. homeland with our allies and partners,” Lohmeier said. “It is clear that our forces project combat-ready airpower in Europe, Africa and beyond, deter aggression, and are prepared to win decisively should deterrence fail.”

items.title: Air Force Recruiting Service meets fiscal 2026 recruiting goals
items.author: Joe Gangemi
items.summary: The Air Force Recruiting Service closed out fiscal year 2026 having met its recruiting goals, enlisting 31,950 U.S. Air Force Airmen and 730 U.S. Space Force Guardians.
items.body:
Published Oct. 1, 2026

By Joe Gangemi

Air Force Accessions Center

The Air Force Recruiting Service closed out fiscal year 2026 having met its recruiting goals, enlisting 31,950 U.S. Air Force Airmen and 730 U.S. Space Force Guardians.

The service, which oversees enlisted and officer accessions for the Air Force and Space Force, credited the results to consistent performance across its recruiting squadrons rather than any single program or push.

"Our recruiters did what they do every year--they worked the mission every day," said Col. Lacresha Merkle, AFRS commander. "Hitting the number is the expectation, and our recruiters delivered."

AFRS recruiting personnel operate out of squadrons across the country, working with applicants through the Delayed Entry Program before they ship to Basic Military Training. The service also supports accessions for career fields ranging from traditional Air Force specialties to Space Force operations.

Looking ahead, fiscal year 2027 planning is already underway, with recruiting strategies adjusted based on labor market trends, propensity-to-serve data and career field demand signals.

"Meeting the mission isn't the finish line--it's the baseline we build on," Merkle said. "Every applicant who signs that contract trusts us with their future, and our recruiters carry that responsibility into every conversation, every single day."

The Air Force Recruiting Service, headquartered at Joint Base San Antonio-Randolph , oversees enlisted, officer and Space Force accessions across the Air Force's total force.

To explore full and part-time opportunities within the Air Force and Space Force, visit www.AirForce.com or www.SpaceForce.com . To speak with a recruiter, click here .

Timetables for operational low flying ( OLF ) training by RAF fast jets and Hercules aircraft. These timetables cover 3 tactical training areas ( TTA ) only. These are:

LFA 7(T): central Wales

LFA 14(T): northern Scotland

LFA 20(T): the borders of southern Scotland and northern England

When the TTA is not in use, there may be other flying activity in the area. The MOD is unable to provide a timetable for all low flying activity as the information can very quickly become outdated due to weather conditions and training requirements.

items.title: Simulating Effects of Methadone Treatment Expansion Policies Using a System Dynamics Model
items.author: Evan D. Peet
items.summary: This report describes the development of a model to analyze policies to address the opioid epidemic and summarizes the relevant data. This paper does not include any specific policy analysis; rather, it presents the tools to do such analysis.
items.body:
Published Oct 1, 2026

This research was made possible by support from The Pew Charitable Trusts and Bloomberg Philanthropies.

Opioids are responsible for tens of thousands of deaths each year, and millions of Americans suffer from opioid use disorder. This report describes the development of a model to analyze policies to address the opioid epidemic and summarizes the relevant data. This paper does not include any specific policy analysis but rather presents the tools to do such analysis.

items.title: The Prospects for Personal Injury Class Actions in the United States
items.author: Elliot Kovnick
items.summary: The authors examine how personal injury class actions have fared since key U.S. Supreme Court rulings, compare those rulings with other litigation aggregation mechanisms, and highlight reforms to support fair and efficient resolution of mass claims.
items.body:
The authors summarize key observations and themes from a panel discussion with experts on the future of personal injury class actions in the United States. Drawing on a discussion of major cases and post-Amchem experience, the authors compare class actions with multidistrict litigation and bankruptcy, highlight trade-offs in oversight and global resolution, and identify reforms that could improve fairness and efficiency in aggregate litigation.

items.title: Accredited official statistics: MOD trade, industry and contracts: 2026
items.summary: Information on Ministry of Defence spending with industry and commerce.
items.body:
This bulletin provides figures on the composition and scope of the department’s expenditure, information on the impact of defence spending on the wider economy, and compares the MOD’s spending to that of other departments and other countries.

The 2026 edition of the Trade, Industry and Contracts bulletin will permanently exclude the section on Major Equipment Projects when published. The underlying data on equipment spending plans had historically been included within the Project Performance Summary Table of the Defence Equipment Plan . However, this data has not been produced since 2024 and the section will now be removed since comparable figures remain unavailable. Note that broadly similar information is provided by the National Infrastructure and Service Transformation Authority (NISTA) in the Major Projects Annual Report .

From 2026, details on defence export orders will be contained solely in the separate UK Defence Export Statistics . Before 2026 this statistical release was published by the Department for Business and Trade (DBT). However, after a Machinery of Government change effective 31 July 2025 , responsibility for defence exports promotion moved from DBT to the MOD. Since MOD now takes full ownership for the production of these statistics, figures will be released in UK Defence Export Statistics only so as to avoid duplication of reporting as well as improve timeliness. The next edition of the export statistics is expected late 2026. Historic data in this time series can still be found in MOD Trade, Industry and Contracts 2025 .

A planned revision of 2026’s Trade, Industry and Contracts bulletin is expected by early 2027. In this revision, the competition and SME status of newly placed contracts in 2025/26 will be reassessed. This is to account for the delayed reporting of new contracts which has historically resulted in a 1% adjustment to the number of contracts reported.

Should you have any comments regarding any of these changes or proposed revisions then please email Analysis-Expenditure-PQ-FOI@mod.gov.uk .

items.title: Santa Monica’s Recent Economic and Social Trends
items.author: Lizhong Liu
items.summary: Researchers compared Santa Monica’s recent economic and social trends with peer cities near Los Angeles. They found steeper declines in retail sales and tourism, but recent policy reforms may improve the city’s economic trajectory.
items.body:
Researchers compared Santa Monica’s recent economic and social trends with peer cities near Los Angeles using data analysis and expert interviews. They found steeper declines in retail sales and tourism, with challenges concentrated downtown. Crime increased in some categories but largely tracks regional trends. The city has recently undertaken substantial reforms in housing, policing, and business development that may improve its outlook.

items.title: Policy Analysis in an Age of Technological and Social Transition
items.author: Anita Chandra
items.summary: In this watershed moment for policy analysis driven by AI, which has eroded trust in experts and institutions, the field must revisit first principles and use them to guide institutional redesign, policy analysis training, and research governance.
items.body:
In this paper, the authors argue that policy analysis is at a watershed moment: AI-driven change, eroding trust in expertise, and shifting configurations of political authority undermine the institutional arrangements that once anchored policy analysis in public life. The field must revisit first principles and use those principles to modernize and guide renewed institutional design, policy analysis training, and research governance.

items.title: Schools, Cell Phones, and AI: Q&A with Melissa Kay Diliberti
items.summary: Melissa Kay Diliberti, an associate policy researcher at RAND, discusses recent findings from RAND that can help parents and policymakers better understand what challenges schools are up against.
items.body:
School is back in session, and that means teachers are once again confronting some familiar challenges. Cell phones tucked into backpacks. Homework that sounds suspiciously like Claude or ChatGPT.

Melissa Kay Diliberti, an associate policy researcher at RAND, has a unique insight into issues like these. It comes from conducting surveys with thousands of teachers, students, parents, and school leaders who participate in RAND survey panels. Through them, Diliberti and other researchers at RAND are able to see what's really happening in the nation's schools.

“Schools are facing a lot of challenges,” Diliberti said. “We see our role as putting numbers to the trends, so education leaders can navigate these challenges with confidence.”

What are some recent findings from RAND that can help parents and policymakers better understand what schools are up against?

Two issues really stand out.

The first is AI. More and more kids in our surveys report that they use AI for school work. A majority of them don't think it's cheating to use AI to look up facts or to get better explanations of their assignments. And it might not be, according to their school rules. But a lot of students are feeling up in the air, asking, “What are the rules here?” Schools have an opportunity—and an obligation—to develop guidance.

The other big one, of course, is cell phones. We asked teens, “How many times are you checking your cell phone in class?” I was surprised, but not shocked, that around 20 percent said they check their phones five or more times a day in class. Another 40 percent said it's one to four times. That's a lot of kids checking their phones during the school day—even in schools that have banned them.

Let's dig into your AI findings first. What do we know about how students are using AI?

The share of students who are using AI is increasing—at the middle school level, the high school level, and the postsecondary level. I don't think that will surprise anyone. But two-thirds of students tell us they have at least some concern that using AI is harming their critical thinking. So even as they're using it, they're thinking about the negative implications of outsourcing too much of their thinking to AI.

How are schools responding to student AI use, and where could they improve?

Schools are starting to get some policies into place. But the technology is moving so fast, it's hard to stay on top of it, and the guidance is lagging and not widely known. We asked kids in December whether their school has any rules on AI use. Only about a third said there were schoolwide rules. A lot of kids said they didn't know. That just underscores the need for very clear guidance from schools on when students can use these tools.

Schools have had more experience with cell phones. How effective have they been at setting boundaries there?

That's one of the biggest questions in education right now. Pretty much all schools have policies restricting cell phone use at this point. But there's very little evidence about how effective these policies have been. We've found that more-restrictive policies may correspond to fewer students checking their phones in class, but this is just based on student self-reports. Maybe not surprisingly, students tell us they're also less likely to check their phones when they know their teachers are strict about enforcing those policies.

Even as they're using it, students are thinking about the negative implications of outsourcing too much of their thinking to AI.

Do students do better at school when they can't check their cell phones?

There's some emerging evidence linking cell phone bans to reduced use of cell phones in schools, and maybe some positive effects on student well-being, at least in the longer term. It's a little unclear if there are any links with student achievement—but again, some evidence that there might be some benefit.

But there are also some real trade-offs. Teachers don't want to spend all day being the phone police. Parents often are skeptical of full phone bans because they want to be able to contact their kids in an emergency. So while there is some evidence that these policies can be good for students, they're not cost-free.

How do you hope your research helps schools navigate these challenges?

Our goal at RAND is to put some real numbers to these nationwide trends, to make sure we understand what's really happening in the school environment. We see a lot of anecdotal evidence in the media about kids using AI to cheat or getting too addicted to their cell phones. But there's not always a lot of data to say how widespread these issues are, how students, parents, or teachers perceive them, or how they're changing.

This is a period of real transition for schools. And it's not just about technology. We see high rates of student absenteeism, high rates of teacher stress. Our goal at RAND, really, is to track these issues and measure them clearly, so policymakers have the information they need to act on them.

items.title: Defenders of the Force: How 121st SFS defenders build strength through struggle
items.author: A1C Samir Harris
items.summary: U.S. Air Force Capt. Jeffrey Lazar, 121st Security Forces Squadron commander, Master Sgt. Sean White, 121st SFS defender, and Airman 1st Class Easton Frost, 121st SFS defender, share their experiences serving as defenders at Alpena Combat Readiness Training Center, Michigan, June 17, 2026. Security forces defenders maintain 24/7 readiness to safeguard force assets, personnel, and combat airpower projection.
items.body:
ALPENA COMBAT READINESS TRAINING CENTER, Mich. — When a Security Forces defender straps on a ballistic vest in the quiet early morning, a slight shift takes place. It isn’t just equipment fastened over standard-issue gear; it’s a commitment to being the barrier between possible threats and the force. For the Airmen of the 121st Security Forces Squadron (SFS), putting on that vest means assuming a role defined by heavy rucks, tough conditions, and an unrelenting duty to protect.

"The mindset you have to step into is to be able to understand that you are the first and last line of defense for protecting the force, to allow combat air power to get into the air," said U.S. Air Force Capt. Jeffrey Lazar, commander of the 121st SFS. "Security forces is a very demanding career field. You're asking young 18-year-old kids to put their lives on the line and make life-or-death decisions at a moment's notice."

Lazar, who served 20 years enlisted before commissioning, understands the job's weight extends far beyond the tactical vest. The drive to push through long hours, extreme heat, and physical exhaustion comes from a devotion to what’s behind the perimeter line.

"As a defender, a lot of times it's not what's in front of us that bothers us; it's the people and the things that we're protecting behind us that keep us going," Lazar said. "It's remembering what's back home that we're protecting—those freedoms and liberties that we are here to preserve."

That drive comes from a shared grit built through brutal field conditions and endless hours on shift. When the rain starts pouring, legs get heavier and heavier, and the gear digs in, all that's left is the plain willpower to keep moving and get the job done.

"High stress in the field is the greatest teacher," said U.S. Air Force Master Sgt. Sean White, a defender with the 121st SFS. "You don't fully understand it until you're doing it in the field, feeling the weather, and feeling the emotions of each other. Those grueling days peel back layers of each person until you're raw, to the fact that you understand each other from a brutal concept."

White, who has served through multiple deployments and field exercises alongside the same Airmen throughout his career, found the unit's real strength in its culture of mutual accountability and personal investment.

"This career field is 100% what you get out of it," White said. "When I put my vest on in the morning, the mindset that I step into is honoring those who have come before me. I look to my left and to my right, and seeing those who wear the same vest motivates me more than anything else."

That shared purpose beats across all ranks, from senior leadership down to the newest Airmen walking onto the flight line. As junior Airmen learn the ropes, they quickly grow under constant pressure and forge a bond with their team that they can’t replicate anywhere else.

"When I put my vest on every morning, I flip the switch—I become a defender," said U.S. Air Force Airman 1st Class Easton Frost, a defender with the 121st SFS. "It means I have to do everything required to make sure the mission gets done. The brotherhood that you get in security forces is really like no other; we become one unit."

Whether balancing tactical decision-making at the command level or managing ground defense in demanding operational conditions, the defenders of the 121st SFS remain bound by a shared identity—one symbolized by the beret they earn and the force they safeguard.

"You aren't a defender until you've earned that badge and earned that beret," Lazar said. "The beret is what signifies and separates us from everybody else. A lot of people—everybody that wears that beret—earned it, and that signifies that we are the defenders of the force."

items.title: DAF awards F-15EX Lot 7 contract for 22 aircraft
items.author: Pentagon News
items.summary: Program negotiators successfully navigated inflation and earlier production disruptions to maintain the full 22-aircraft buy before the fiscal year-end deadline.
items.body:
Published Sept. 29, 2026

Air Force Life Cycle Management Center’s Fighters and Advanced Aircraft Directorate

The Department of the Air Force awarded Boeing a contract for 22 F-15EX Eagle II aircraft under Lot 7 — preserving the buying power of congressionally provided reconciliation funding and sustaining F-15EX production. The Lot 7 agreement accounts for current programmatic realities, including the effects of the 2025 production disruption and broader inflation across the defense industrial base. Through focused, complex negotiations, the F-15 Program Office and Boeing reached an agreement that maintains the procurement of all 22 Lot 7 aircraft within available funding. "Lot 7 reflects a disciplined approach to executing available resources while balancing the realities affecting defense production," said Brig. Gen. Timothy Helfrich , portfolio acquisition executive for the Fighters and Advanced Aircraft Directorate . "The team remained focused on affordability, production continuity and delivering the aircraft needed to modernize the U.S. Air Force’s fighter fleet for the threats we face today and into the future." The F-15EX is a modern, multirole heavy fighter that builds on the proven F-15 design. The aircraft incorporates advanced avionics, large-area displays, digital backbone architecture and enhanced survivability capabilities. It is intended to replace aging F-15C and F-15D aircraft while providing a platform for continued modernization as operational requirements evolve. The Lot 7 award also demonstrates the application of the Secretary of War's acquisition transformation principles by empowering an integrated F-15 negotiation team to rapidly deliver capability. The team synchronized expertise across functional areas, elevated issues requiring senior-level decisions, and maintained accountability for cost, schedule, and aircraft quantity — demonstrating the speed, disciplined execution, and mission-focused accountability central to the warfighting acquisition system. This award followed extensive collaboration among program management, contracting, pricing, engineering, financial management, logistics and other acquisition professionals. The team assessed the impacts of changing production conditions and inflation, aligned the aircraft procurement with available funding, and completed the action before the fiscal-year deadline. Senior department leaders supported timely coordination and decision-making throughout the process. Their engagement enabled the team to address complex affordability and execution challenges while maintaining focus on the program’s operational purpose: delivering modern fighter capability to Airmen. "The Lot 7 award demonstrates what is possible when the acquisition enterprise moves with purpose, remains accountable to the taxpayer and stays focused on delivering capability to the warfighter," said Col. Jonathan Varoli, system program manager of the directorate's F-15 Program Office. "This effort brought together the right expertise, at the right time, to achieve an outcome that strengthens the F-15EX program and supports the future fighter force." The Department of the Air Force will continue working with Boeing to support rapid, affordable and sustainable F-15EX production. The Lot 7 award sustains the program’s near-term production effort while the Air Force continues to assess future requirements and acquisition strategies.

items.title: Air Force advances point defense enterprise with plans for new weapon system, career field
items.author: Pentagon News
items.summary: The U.S. Air Force is advancing point defense as a core function of air and space power, strengthening its ability to protect the Airmen, aircraft, infrastructure and other critical assets required to generate combat airpower.
items.body:
Published Sept. 29, 2026

Secretary of the Air Force Public Affairs

The U.S. Air Force is advancing point defense as a core function of air and space power, strengthening its ability to protect the Airmen, aircraft, infrastructure and other critical assets required to generate combat airpower. Chief of Staff of the Air Force Gen. Ken Wilsbach announced two related initiatives during his Sept. 14 keynote address at the 2026 Air and Space Forces Association Air, Space & Cyber Conference: establishment of the Point Defense Weapon System and development of a dedicated career field for point defense Airmen. “Ultimately, point defense is about preserving our ability to generate combat airpower,” Lt. Gen. Case Cunningham , Air Force deputy chief of staff for operations, said. “We’re building the Airmen, the systems and the integrated command and control necessary to keep our bases operating and our aircraft flying in the face of attack.” The Point Defense Weapon System will be an integrated system-of-systems designed to connect sensors, command and control and layered kinetic and non-kinetic capabilities to detect, track and defeat airborne threats before they can disrupt installation operations. Rather than a single platform, the weapon system will provide an enterprise-wide framework capable of integrating new capabilities as threats, technologies and operational requirements evolve. Point defense is an established military concept focused on protecting specific areas or critical assets from attack. The Air Force’s April 2025 “ Point Defense of Air Bases Doctrine Advisory ,” which builds on existing Air Force and joint doctrine, describes how installation-level defensive capabilities complement and integrate with the broader joint air and missile defense architecture. The Air Force also plans to establish a new career field of point defense Airmen, with the goal of becoming operational within two years. These Airmen will develop specialized expertise in operating and integrating sensors, command and control, and layered defensive capabilities. They will work alongside Security Forces and other Air Force and joint mission partners to deliver coordinated and layered defense of installations. “Establishing a new career field is about more than creating a specialty code,” Lt. Gen. Jefferson O’Donnell , Air Force deputy chief of staff for manpower, personnel and services, said. “We must build a professional community with the right training, experience, and career development to deliver this capability over time. Success is an Air Force where Airmen—recruited, trained, developed, and retained as point defense specialists—strengthen the Air Force's ability to fight and win.” The effort builds upon the Air Force’s established integrated defense approach, which brings together installation capabilities to protect personnel, resources and combat operations. Security Forces provide essential expertise in planning and executing integrated defense, while the new career field will add dedicated expertise to help integrate point defense capabilities into the broader defensive architecture. “Our Security Forces Airmen have built a legacy of excellence in integrated defense,” Lt. Gen. Kenyon Bell , Air Force deputy chief of staff for logistics, engineering and force protection, said. “They understand how to bring capabilities together to protect our installations and keep the mission going. Point defense builds on that foundation, integrating our defenders with specialized point defense forces to create an even more effective, layered defense.” To strengthen integration between the two career fields, a Security Forces Airman will serve as deputy career field manager for point defense, helping to align training, professional development and operational expertise across both communities. The point defense enterprise must also integrate beyond the installation. In the homeland, these capabilities will connect with existing air defense arrangements and operate within applicable airspace and engagement authorities. During contingency operations and conflict, they will integrate with the theater’s joint air and missile defense architecture, ensuring local defensive capabilities contribute to, and benefit from, the broader air picture. “Defense of our air bases cannot occur in isolation from the airspace around them,” Lt. Gen. Case Cunningham, Air Force deputy chief of staff for operations, said. “Our sensors, command and control and defensive tools must connect to the broader air defense network, whether we’re defending an installation in the homeland or a forward operating location in conflict. We need to contribute to that larger picture and benefit from what the joint force sees, giving commanders the information and options they need to employ the right effect at the right time.” The Point Defense Weapon System is being designed to evolve rapidly as new technologies emerge and operating environments change. “We need a weapon system that can adapt as quickly as the threat,” said Lt. Gen. Christopher Niemi , Air Force deputy chief of staff for force modernization and chief modernization officer. “That means building an open, modular architecture that allows us to rapidly integrate new sensors and defensive tools, adapt to different operating environments and remain connected to the broader defensive network.” The Air Force is in the early stages of developing both the Point Defense Weapon System and career field. Additional implementation details will be announced as the service refines requirements, training, force development and integration plans.

items.title: AFLCMC commander outlines acquisition priorities at Ohio Defense and Aerospace Forum
items.author: Patrick Londergan
items.summary: DAYTON, Ohio (AFLCMC) -- “You are part of the fight,” Lt. Gen. Jason Voorheis, commander of the Air Force Life Cycle Management Center (AFLCMC) told attendees at the Ohio Defense and Aerospace Forum earlier this week. “ General Dale White [Director, Critical Major Weapon Systems at the Pentagon] is fond of saying that militaries don't go to war - nations go to war. You all are part of what our nation brings to the fight in terms of developing fielding and getting capability into the hands of our
items.body:
DAYTON, Ohio (AFLCMC) -- “You are part of the fight,” Lt. Gen. Jason Voorheis, commander of the Air Force Life Cycle Management Center (AFLCMC) told attendees at the Ohio Defense and Aerospace Forum earlier this week. “ General Dale White [Director, Critical Major Weapon Systems at the Pentagon] is fond of saying that militaries don't go to war - nations go to war. You all are part of what our nation brings to the fight in terms of developing fielding and getting capability into the hands of our warfighters.”

Voorheis spoke as part of a panel titled “Power Projection from the Heartland.” He was joined on stage by Brig. Gen. Timothy Helfrich, AFLCMC Portfolio Acquisition Executive (PAE) for Fighters and Advanced Aircraft, alongside defense industry professionals TK Kubit and Anthony Cain. JP Nauseef of JobsOhio moderated the discussion. The forum was hosted by the Dayton Development Coalition.

Held at Wright State University on September 21, 2026, the forum highlighted the strategic alignment between Air Force modernization priorities and the Ohio defense ecosystem.

Acquisition Speed and Agility

The Ohio Defense Ecosystem

Workforce and Talent Development

In his opening remarks, Voorheis explained the Air Force acquisition workforce's shift to accept risk earlier, lean into commercial technology and open mission systems, and empower program teams to make decisions that drive projects forward.

Both Voorheis and Helfrich noted that acquisition teams at Wright-Patt and across the Center are transitioning away from platform-specific "stovepipes" to focus on broader, integrated capabilities across advanced aircraft. These teams are also balancing intensive current fleet modernization with future systems development by shifting from individual platform upgrades to an integrated, "system of systems" approach.

“I think one of the really important parts about the acquisition transformation is the change in philosophy and focus on delivering fielded capability as kind of the preeminent prioritized pacing thing that we do, and everything else is about how we achieve that to include the authorities we're giving PAEs,” noted Voorheis.

Helfrich’s Fighters and Advanced Aircraft portfolio includes the A-10, F-15, F-16, F-22, plus the FQ-42, FQ-44, other collaborative combat aircraft.

The Air Force Research Lab (AFRL) is also headquartered at Wright-Patt. Helfrich touted how AFRL led key advances in open architecture and credits AFRL with developing the Collaborative Combat Aircraft (CCA) program.

“There would be no CCA without the Air Force Research Laboratory,” explained Helfrich. “Both the FQ-42 Vengeance [and] the FQ-44 Fury were heavily invested in by AFRL. Because software is sold separately with CCA, the mission autonomy work started at AFRL. They were really the ones who put together the first consortium to build Autonomous Government Reference Architecture (A-GRA). This has become a huge program, all made possible because of the investments by AFRL.”

For both Voorheis and Helfrich, the workforce and supporting infrastructure remain top concerns. Helfrich urged educators in the audience to modernize military engineering and software development classes. Both speakers noted the shortage of physical defense infrastructure in the area around Wright-Patterson, particularly for high-level classified work.

In addition to physical plant limitations, hiring remains a challenge. AFLCMC currently has over 1,700 vacancies , with more than half located at Wright-Patt. Most open positions are in technical fields like engineering and logistics. Business areas like contracting and program management also have many openings.

“We need help recruiting from the universities and from industry as well, both defense industry and non-defense industry,” explained Voorheis. “You don't have to come in with a lot of aerospace experience. What we really need is highly talented, motivated, critical thinkers.”

The panel marked the first time Lt. Gen. Voorheis has publicly spoken about his role leading AFLCMC since assuming command late last month .
items.titleZh: AFLCMC司令在俄亥俄州国防与航空航天论坛上阐述采办优先事项
items.summaryZh: 俄亥俄州代顿（AFLCMC）——“你们也是这场战斗的一部分，”美国空军生命周期管理中心（AFLCMC）司令Lt. Gen.贾森·沃希斯（Jason Voorheis）本周早些时候在俄亥俄州国防与航空航天论坛上对与会者表示。“Gen.戴尔·怀特（五角大楼关键重大武器系统主管）喜欢说，参战的不是军队——而是国家。你们所有人都是我们国家投入这场战斗的一部分，体现在研发、列装并把能力交到我们的……手中。”
items.zhFull:
代顿，俄亥俄州（AFLCMC）——“你们是战斗的一部分，”美国空军生命周期管理中心（AFLCMC）司令 Lt. Gen. 贾森·沃里斯（Jason Voorheis）本周早些时候在俄亥俄国防与航空航天论坛上对与会者说。“戴尔·怀特将军（Dale White）[五角大楼关键重大武器系统主管]喜欢说，军队不会开战——国家才会开战。你们所有人都是我国为这场战斗所贡献力量的一部分，无论是开发、列装，还是把能力交到我们的作战人员手中。”

沃里斯作为题为“来自腹地的力量投射”的专题讨论小组成员发言。与他同台的有 Brig. Gen. 蒂莫西·赫尔弗里希（Timothy Helfrich），AFLCMC 战斗机与先进飞机组合采办执行官（PAE），以及国防工业专业人士 TK·库比特（TK Kubit）和安东尼·凯恩（Anthony Cain）。JobsOhio 的 JP·诺西夫（JP Nauseef）主持了讨论。该论坛由代顿发展联盟主办。

论坛于2026年9月21日在莱特州立大学举行，凸显了空军现代化优先事项与俄亥俄国防生态系统之间的战略协同。

采办速度与敏捷性

俄亥俄国防生态系统

劳动力与人才发展

沃里斯在开场致辞中解释说，空军采办队伍正在转变，更早接受风险，积极采用商业技术和开放任务系统，并赋予项目团队作出推动项目前进的决策的权力。

沃里斯和赫尔弗里希都指出，Wright-Patt 以及整个中心的采办团队正从针对特定平台的“烟囱式”模式转向，专注于先进飞机更广泛的一体化能力。这些团队还在平衡当前密集的机队现代化与未来系统开发，从单个平台升级转向一体化的“系统之系统”方法。

“我认为采办转型真正重要的部分之一，是理念的转变，以及把交付已列装能力作为我们最重要的优先事项和节奏牵引，而其他一切——包括我们赋予PAE的权限——都是为了实现这一目标，”沃海斯（Voorheis）指出。

赫尔弗里希（Helfrich）的“战斗机与先进飞机”组合包括A-10、F-15、F-16、F-22，以及FQ-42、FQ-44和其他协同作战飞机。

美国空军研究实验室（AFRL）也总部设在赖特-帕特森（Wright-Patt）。赫尔弗里希盛赞AFRL在开放架构方面引领了关键进展，并将协同作战飞机（CCA）项目的发展归功于AFRL。

“没有美国空军研究实验室，就不会有CCA，”赫尔弗里希解释道。“AFRL对FQ-42‘复仇’和FQ-44‘狂怒’都投入了大量资金。由于CCA的软件是单独销售的，任务自主性工作始于AFRL。他们确实是组建首个联盟来构建自主政府参考架构（A-GRA）的一方。这已成为一个庞大的项目，而这一切都得益于AFRL的投资。”

对沃海斯和赫尔弗里希而言，劳动力和配套基础设施仍是首要关切。赫尔弗里希敦促在场教育工作者对军事工程和软件开发课程进行现代化改革。两位发言人都指出，赖特-帕特森周边地区缺乏实体国防基础设施，尤其是用于高级别机密工作的设施。

除实体设施限制外，招聘仍是一项挑战。美国空军生命周期管理中心（AFLCMC）目前有超过1,700个职位空缺，其中一半以上位于赖特-帕特森。大多数空缺职位属于工程和后勤等技术领域。合同签订和项目管理等业务领域也有许多空缺。

“我们需要在从大学以及产业界招聘方面获得帮助，既包括国防产业，也包括非国防产业，”沃海斯解释道。“你不需要带着丰富的航空航天经验入职。我们真正需要的是才华出众、积极进取、善于批判性思考的人。”

此次小组讨论标志着Lt. Gen.沃海斯自上月底就任指挥官以来，首次公开谈及他领导AFLCMC的职责。

items.body:
The Air Force Research Laboratory (AFRL) has five unique ionizing radiation sources. All sources are maintained and operated by the Survivable Electronics Technology group (AFRL/RJSV) at Kirtland AFB, NM. These sources allow partnering researchers from industry, government labs, and universities to study a wide spectrum of total ionizing dose and prompt dose effects. The Survivable Electronics Technology group primarily uses these sources to determine the effects of radiation on advanced microelectronics, photonics, sensors, and micro-electromechanical systems needed for Air Force, Space Force, Department of Defense, and government space and missile systems .

Dosimetry; both CaF 2 and Ion Chambers

Fabricate test board and boxes for devices under test

Machine Shop access

B1500 w/ Switching Matrix

Mixed Signal Tester

Gamma Radiation Sources

The Cobalt-60 source can deliver a maximum total ionizing dose of ~20 krad (Si)/min to a minimum of <1 rad (Si)/min (which falls within ASTM 1019 specs of 300 to 50 rad(Si)/sec). Slightly higher dose rates may be attained if researchers are willing to accept that the source will appear as a line source opposed to a point source. This source produces two energy peaks at 1.17 and 1.33 MeV. The irradiator is a 360-degree panoramic irradiator, facility area is 1,500 ft 2 which provides the researcher the benefit of a large range of variable dose rates with plenty of area to conduct experiments. Evaluation of subsystems is possible in this cell. The large area of the facility minimizes the possibility of dose enhancement due to scatter. The high energy photons give a uniform dose deposition throughout the sample of interest. AFRL Co-60 facility provides the capability of performing in-situ experiments whereby measurements on components are taken during gamma irradiation through the use of 120 ft of BNC cables and CAT-5 cables that would allow the experimenters to control computer-controlled instrumentation from the control room to the irradiation test cell.

Total Dose Simulator

1.17 & 1.33 MeV Gammas

<.001 to 20 krad(Si)/min

1500 ft 2 of Test Cell

360-degree panoramic irradiator

The Cesium 137 low dose rate source will deliver a maximum of 40 rad(Si)/hr or a minimum of 0.3 rad(Si)/hr. This source produces gamma rays with a single energy peak at 662 keV. The Cs-137 source is capable of housing experiments which can fit in 1 ft 3 of volume. Due to the small exposure volume, a Pb/Al box is required for all experiments performed in this source to eliminate a dose enhancement effect. Will provide a Pb/Al box for experiments which meets ASTM standards if users do not have one. This source is capable of providing in-situ experimentation.

Low Total Dose Simulator

662 keV Gammas

0.005 to 0.667 rad(Si)/min

2.25 ft 2 Test Cell

X-Ray Radiation Sources

The ARACOR X-ray test system is used to investigate total ionizing dose effects on individual microelectronic devices. This system produces X-rays with energies that have a max range of 60 keV with peak energies at 10 keV and dose rates ranging from 0.1 to 30 krad (SiO 2 )/min. The system is capable to accommodating an 8” wafer for X-ray characterization of fabricated die or packaged devices with lids removed. Capable of utilizing a probe card to probe and bias up to 48 contacts concurrently.

10 to 60 keV spectrum, peak 10 keV

0.1 to 30 krad (SiO 2 )/min

Low Energy X-Ray (LEXR)

The Low Energy X-ray source is a Comet MXR-160/22 constant potential X-ray system which produces X-rays with energies that have a max range of 10 keV to 160 keV and peaks at 10 keV and 60 keV depending on the applied voltage. This source can produce a total ionizing dose rate of 360 krad (SiO 2 )/min. Exposure area is a 1.84 cm diameter at 10 cm from the X-ray tube. The distance from the tube can be varied up to 1 m to control dose rate. The X-ray tube current is variable in order to control dose rate, and the total energy deposited per unit area. This source is capable of providing in-situ experimentation.

High Total Dose Simulator

10 to 160 keV spectrum, peaks 10 and 60 keV(adjustable)

360 krad(SiO 2 )/min (max)

30 ft 2 Test Cell

Flash X-Ray (FXR)

The Flash X-ray source is a Febetron 705 machine which produces prompt dose exposures simulating nuclear weapons environments. This facility is capable of producing a 20 nanosecond pulse X-ray. The average 2.1 MeV of the X-rays produced in this facility provides a dose rate output from between 1x10 7 to 2x10 11 rad (Si)/sec. A 70 ft 2 . screen room is available for housing experiments in order to minimize the effects of EMP produced by the Febetron 705. To obtain higher dose rates, experiments may be performed in open air directly in front of the Febetron 705.

High Dose Simulator

X-ray Mode (Prompt dose)

1x10 7 to 2x10 11 rad(Si)/sec X-ray

items.title: AFRL demonstrates modular multimode propulsion system for sustained space maneuver
items.author: Patrick Londergan
items.summary: EDWARDS AIR FORCE BASE, Calif. -- The Air Force Research Laboratory (AFRL) recently demonstrated an innovative spacecraft propulsion system under realistic conditions in a specialized test facility at Edwards Air Force Base, California. “This work helps advance propulsion technologies that will give future space operators more flexible options for maneuver to adapt and sustain operations in demanding environments, as is required by U.S. Space Command,” said Dr. Andrew Williams , director of the
items.body:
EDWARDS AIR FORCE BASE, Calif. -- The Air Force Research Laboratory (AFRL) recently demonstrated an innovative spacecraft propulsion system under realistic conditions in a specialized test facility at Edwards Air Force Base, California.

“This work helps advance propulsion technologies that will give future space operators more flexible options for maneuver to adapt and sustain operations in demanding environments, as is required by U.S. Space Command,” said Dr. Andrew Williams , director of the AFRL Space Warfare Directorate .

Termed Propulsion Optimization UNifying Chemical and Electric (POUNCE), the demonstration proved the capability of an innovative propulsion technology called Modular Multimode Propulsion (MMP). MMP features both electric and chemical propulsion using the same propellant along with a single tank and feed system. Electric propulsion enables high-efficiency, low-thrust, long-duration and slow maneuvers; chemical propulsion enables shorter-duration, higher-thrust and faster maneuvers.

For the team behind POUNCE, the effort is not just about proving a concept—it is about giving future operators more flexible tools to meet mission demands in space.

“This demonstration is a pioneering leap in the advancement of flexible, modular and high-performance space propulsion technology to enable dynamic space operations,” said Dr. Javier Urzay, AFRL Rocket and Space Propulsion Division chief. “Our goal is to bring the future faster and deliver integrated capabilities for space warfare.”

The MMP architecture reduces system mass and volume, while increasing operational flexibility and resilience. It provides operators with discretion to allocate the same propellant to high-tempo maneuvers or more efficient repositioning of orbital assets.

The propellant used for the MMP system in this demonstration was the AFRL-developed Advanced Spacecraft Energetic Non-Toxic (ASCENT) fuel. AFRL has pursued several technology maturation activities jointly with industry to exploit the higher-density specific impulse and safer handling of ASCENT for spacecraft propulsion.

POUNCE’s MMP system also incorporated hardware from industry partners, including a composite conformal tank and propellant feed system from Flight Works, chemical thrusters from Igneon Aerospace, and a PALOMINO ion array electrospray thruster from Revolution Space.

“Alongside the relationships with our commercial partners, another equally important ingredient for this demonstration is the unique capabilities offered by the Space Propulsion Environment Facility (SPEF) at the AFRL Rocket Lab at Edwards AFB,” said Dr. Gregory Yandek, AFRL In-Space Propulsion Branch chief.

Inside SPEF, researchers were able to expose the experimental MMP system to the high-vacuum characteristics of orbital environments. Theorists first conceptualized the dual-mode combination of low-thrust and high-thrust propulsion capabilities for space missions in the 1960s, but experimentation with hardware has been limited to single-mode or primitive components until now.

Finally, the POUNCE MMP demonstration highlights how leveraging public-private partnerships can accelerate the transition of technology concepts toward operationally relevant capabilities. The demonstration hardware featured a highly modular design to quickly and easily swap different propulsion subsystems without having to change the parent system. This extra layer of flexibility will greatly increase system life replenishment and space maneuver capabilities in future operating environments.

The Air Force Research Laboratory is the Department of the Air Force’s primary scientific research and development center and one of six centers within Air Force Materiel Command. AFRL leads the discovery, development and delivery of technologies for air, space and multidomain. With a workforce spanning seven mission areas at more than 40 locations worldwide, AFRL conducts research ranging from basic science to advanced technology development. For more information, visit afresearchlab.com .
